## Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Monument_of_the_Discoveries&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Architecture")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Rosa-dos-ventos.JPG/250px-Rosa-dos-ventos.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rosa-dos-ventos.JPG)

The [compass rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compass_rose "Compass rose") and [mappa mundi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mappa_mundi "Mappa mundi"), a gift from the [Union of South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_South_Africa "Union of South Africa") created from beige, black and red limestone. [Jerónimos Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jer%C3%B3nimos_Monastery "Jerónimos Monastery") is in the background.

The structure is located on the northern bank of the [Tagus River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus_River "Tagus River"), neighboring the Belém Marina, Algés and Dafundo Nautical Centre, and the Museum of Popular Art ([Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"): _Museu de Arte Popular_), and demarcated by stone pedestals with [armillary spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armillary_sphere "Armillary sphere").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_to_the_Discoveries#cite_note-SIPA-1) Opposite the large square, and across the Avenida da Índia-Avenida de Brasília motorway, is the _Praça do Império_ (Empire Square) which fronts the [Jerónimos Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jer%C3%B3nimos_Monastery "Jerónimos Monastery"), [Belém Cultural Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Cultural_Center "Belém Cultural Center") and the green-spaces of the _Jardim Vasco da Gama_.

The original structure, which Telmo, Barros and Almeida created, was erected in steel and cement, while the 33 statues were produced in a composite of [plaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaster "Plaster") and [tow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tow_(fibre) "Tow (fibre)"). Ostensibly a 56-metre-high (184 ft) slab standing vertically along the bank of the Tagus, the design takes the form of the [prow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prow "Prow") of a [caravel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravel "Caravel") (ship used in the early Portuguese exploration). On either side of the slab are ramps that join at the river's edge, with the figure of Henry the Navigator on its edge. On either side of the [Infante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infante "Infante"), along the ramp, are 16 figures (33 in total) representing figures from the Portuguese [Age of Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discovery "Age of Discovery"). These great people of the era included [monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchs "Monarchs"), [explorers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explorer "Explorer"), [cartographers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartographer "Cartographer"), [artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artist "Artist"), [scientists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientist "Scientist") and [missionaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missionary "Missionary"). Each idealized figure is designed to show movement towards the front (the unknown sea), projecting a direct or indirect synthesis of their participation in the events after Henry.

The [South African government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") was responsible for gifting the construction of the square in front of the monument: the 50-metre-diameter (160 ft)_Rosa-dos-Ventos_ (_[compass rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compass\_rose "Compass rose")_) was executed using different types of [limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone "Limestone"), including lioz, a rare type of beige limestone found only around Lisbon, more specifically in Sintra.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_to_the_Discoveries#cite_note-SIPA-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_to_the_Discoveries#cite_note-EGEACp-3) Designed by the architect Cristino da Silva, it includes a [Mappa mundi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mappa_mundi "Mappa mundi") that is 14 metres wide, showing the routes of Portuguese [carracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrack "Carrack") and caravels during the Age of Discovery.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_to_the_Discoveries#cite_note-SIPA-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_to_the_Discoveries#cite_note-EGEACp-3)

On the northern façade flanking the staircase are two inscriptions in metal: on the left, _"AO INFANTE D. HENRIQVE E AOS PORTVGVESES QVE DESCOBRIRAM OS CAMINHOS DO MAR"_ (_To Prince Lord Henry and the Portuguese that Discovered the Paths of the Sea_) over a metal anchor; and, on the right, the words _"NO V CENTENÁRIO DO INFANTE D. HENRIQVE 1460 – 1960"_ (_On the Fifth centenary of Prince Lord Henry 1460–1960_), over a crown of [laurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_wreath "Laurel wreath").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_to_the_Discoveries#cite_note-SIPA-1) The double staircase ascends one level, before the entranceway to the monument, allowing a perspective on the square and the lateral figures.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_to_the_Discoveries#cite_note-SIPA-1)

The interior consists of three areas: the auditorium with space for 101 people, a stage of 18 square metres (190 sq ft), with film projection booth; a secondary level with two halls for exhibition; and the last level with four rooms.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_to_the_Discoveries#cite_note-SIPA-1) Normally, the auditorium hosts a multimedia exhibition on the history of [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), while the other rooms are used for exhibitions. The top of the monument (reached via a lift or stairs) offers views of the Tagus river, the Belém neighbourhood and its many attractions, including the [Belém Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower "Belém Tower") and the [Jerónimos Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jer%C3%B3nimos_Monastery "Jerónimos Monastery"), which date from the _Age of Discovery_.

**Belém Tower** (Portuguese: _Torre de Belém_, pronounced[[ˈtoʁɨ ðɨ βɨˈlɐ̃j]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Portuguese "Help:IPA/Portuguese"); literally: [Bethlehem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem "Bethlehem") Tower), officially the **Tower of [Saint Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_of_Saragossa "Vincent of Saragossa")** (Portuguese: _Torre de São Vicente_), is a 16th-century fortification located in [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), Portugal, which served as a point of embarkation and disembarkation for Portuguese explorers and as a ceremonial gateway to Lisbon.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-DHA-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-UNESCO2019-3) The tower symbolizes Portugal's maritime and colonial power in early modern Europe. It was built during the height of the [Portuguese Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Renaissance "Portuguese Renaissance") and is a prominent example of the Portuguese [Manueline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manueline "Manueline") style,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Lach-4) but it also incorporates other architectural styles, such as the minarets, which are inspired by [Moorish architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorish_architecture "Moorish architecture").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Portugal_tourism-5) The structure was built from [lioz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lioz "Lioz")[limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone "Limestone"), a material local to the Lisbon region,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-6) and is composed of a [bastion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion "Bastion") and a 30-metre (100 ft)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Watson-7) four-storey tower.

Since 1983, the tower has been a UNESCO [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site"), along with the [Jerónimos Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jer%C3%B3nimos_Monastery "Jerónimos Monastery"). It is often portrayed as a symbol of Europe's [Age of Discoveries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discoveries "Age of Discoveries")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-UNESCO2019-3) and as a metonym for [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal") or Lisbon, given its landmark status. It has incorrectly been stated that the tower was built in the middle of the Tagus and now sits near the shore because the river was redirected after the [1755 Lisbon earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake "1755 Lisbon earthquake"). In fact, the tower was built on a small island in the [Tagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus "Tagus") river near the Lisbon shore.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Portugal_tourism-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR-8)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bel%C3%A9m_Tower&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Lisbon_Torre_de_Bel%C3%A9m_BW_2018-10-03_16-34-03.jpg/250px-Lisbon_Torre_de_Bel%C3%A9m_BW_2018-10-03_16-34-03.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lisbon_Torre_de_Bel%C3%A9m_BW_2018-10-03_16-34-03.jpg)

The tower was classified as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983 and included in the registry of the [Seven Wonders of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Wonders_of_Portugal "Seven Wonders of Portugal") in 2007.

In the late 15th century, [King John II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_Portugal "John II of Portugal") had designed a defence system for the mouth of the Tagus that depended on the fortresses of [Cascais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cascais "Cascais") and _São Sebastião_ (or _Torre Velha_) in [Caparica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caparica_(Almada) "Caparica (Almada)") on the south side of the river.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Portugal_tourism-5)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBTorre-9) These fortresses did not completely protect the river's mouth, and further protection was required.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBTorre-9) In his "Chronicle of [John II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_Portugal "John II of Portugal")" (_Chronica de D. Joao II_), which appeared in 1545,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Hirsch1967-10) the author [Garcia de Resende](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garcia_de_Resende "Garcia de Resende") affirmed the king's opinion that the defences of Lisbon were inadequate, and that he had insisted on building fortifications along the entrance to the River [Tagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus "Tagus") to supplement the existing defences.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11) To this end, he ordered the "making of a strong fort", but died before any plans were drawn. King [Manuel I of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_I_of_Portugal "Manuel I of Portugal") revisited the proposal twenty years later and ordered the construction of a military fortification on the northern margin of the Tagus at Belém.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBTorre-9) In 1513, Lourenço Fernandes wrote a letter to his friends referring to the king's intention of constructing a tower near Restelo Velho, having determined it to be essential.

The presence of this military element was also a celebration of the round trip of the Portuguese to India and a way of receiving the fleets that arrived at the mouth of the Tagus, glorifying the feat, as if it were a mimetic of what those who arrived could identify with what they had seen in the East. The best example is the carved rhinoceros, the result of an offer from an Indian ruler who offered it to King Dom Manuel. This Rhinoceros would be the same one that [Albrecht Dürer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albrecht_D%C3%BCrer "Albrecht Dürer") would immortalize in his drawings.

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Portuguese_India_16-17th_centuries_v05.jpg/330px-Portuguese_India_16-17th_centuries_v05.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portuguese_India_16-17th_centuries_v05.jpg)

Portuguese presence in India, the Gulf of Bengal and the Himalayas (maximum extent) between the 15th and 17th centuries

The project was started on a basaltic rock outcrop a short distance from the riverbank, using some of the stone being collected to build the [Monastery of Santa Maria de Belém](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jer%C3%B3nimos_Monastery "Jerónimos Monastery"). The tower was designed by military architect [Francisco de Arruda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_de_Arruda "Francisco de Arruda"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Hourihane2012-12) named "Master of the works of the Belém stronghold" by King Manuel,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Almeida1992-13) and in 1516 he began receiving 763 blocks and 504 stones for its construction, delivered by Diogo Rodrigues, treasurer for the project. As construction progressed, a man-of-war called the _Grande Nau_ (Great Ship), a heavily armed, 1000–ton ship continued to guard the estuary at the mouth of the Tagus until the fort's completion.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR_Tower-15)

The building was finished in 1519, just two years before Manuel's death, and Gaspar de Paiva was temporarily stationed to command the fortress;[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-16) his commission was made permanent on 15 September 1521, when he was appointed the first Captain-General, or [alcalde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcalde "Alcalde"), and the fortress was named the Castle of St Vincent (_Castelo de São Vicente de Belém_),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Torre-17) in honour of the patron saint of Lisbon.

In 1571, [Francisco de Holanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_de_Holanda "Francisco de Holanda") advised the monarch that it was necessary to improve the coastal defences in order to protect the kingdom's capital. He suggested the construction of a "strong and impregnable" fort that could easily defend Lisbon and that the Belém Tower "should be strengthened, repaired and completed...that it has cost so much without being completed". D'Holanda designed an improved rectangular bastion with several turrets. In 1580, after a few hours of battle, the garrison stationed in the tower surrendered to Spanish forces under the command of the [Duke of Alba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fadrique_%C3%81lvarez_de_Toledo,_4th_Duke_of_Alba "Fadrique Álvarez de Toledo, 4th Duke of Alba"). After this defeat, the dungeons of the tower served as a prison until 1830.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Torre-17) It was also during the last quarter of the 16th century that the construction of the Philippine Barracks began. A rectangular two-storey space was constructed over the bastion, giving the tower the visual profile that it has retained to the present, with sculpted crosses of the [Order of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Christ_(Portugal) "Order of Christ (Portugal)") and domed turrets.

In 1589, [Philip I of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_I_of_Portugal "Philip I of Portugal") ordered Italian engineer Friar João Vicenzio Casale to build a well-defended fort to be constructed in place of the "useless castle of São Vicente".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11) The engineer submitted three designs, proposing that the bastion would be surrounded by another bastion of greater dimensions, but the project never materialized.

A 1633 codex for the House of Cadaval was inserted into one of the floors, in one of the arches of the barracks, and in the four largest arches at the top of the southern façade. Similarly, a reference to the year 1655 was inscribed on a plaque placed on the northern wall of the cloister, which certified the tower's function as a customs control point and for navigation along the Tagus; vessels were obliged to pay a tax as they entered the harbour, which was imposed incrementally.

Between 1780 and 1782, under the reign of [Maria I of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_I_of_Portugal "Maria I of Portugal"), General Guilherme de Valleré constructed the [Fort of Bom Sucesso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_of_Bom_Sucesso "Fort of Bom Sucesso"), whose battery was connected by a western corridor wall to the tower.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11) When French forces invaded Lisbon during the [Peninsular War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peninsular_War "Peninsular War"), detachments of their troops were quartered in the tower from 1808 to 1814. After the French retreated, [Lord Beresford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Beresford,_1st_Viscount_Beresford "William Beresford, 1st Viscount Beresford") advised that coastal artillery batteries should be reinforced along the Tagus, and specifically noted that stronger batteries should be placed on the sides of the tower's bastion, with carts placed to better protect the soldiers, since the walls were very low.

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Combat_du_Tage.jpg/250px-Combat_du_Tage.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Combat_du_Tage.jpg)

French ships exchanging fire with the tower during the [Battle of the Tagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Tagus_(1831) "Battle of the Tagus (1831)") of the [Liberal Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Wars "Liberal Wars")

[King Miguel I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_of_Portugal "Miguel of Portugal") (1828–1834) used the dungeons to imprison his liberal opponents,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Watson-7) while another level was used as a [custom house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Custom_house "Custom house") for ships until the duty on foreign ships was abolished in 1833.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Torre-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Penny-18) The tower received military upgrades in 1589 and 1809–1814.

During the reign of [Maria II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_II_of_Portugal "Maria II of Portugal"), [Almeida Garrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almeida_Garrett "Almeida Garrett") protested the site's degradation and under the persuasion of the [Duke of Terceira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_Jos%C3%A9_Severim_de_Noronha,_1st_Duke_of_Terceira "António José Severim de Noronha, 1st Duke of Terceira"), renovations were begun by military engineer António de Azevedo e Cunha.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11) He demolished the Philippine barracks and extended revivalist elements in 1845–46 (such as the armoured merlons, the [balustrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baluster "Baluster") of the veranda along the southern façade, the laced fascia in the cloister and the niche with an image of the [Virgin and Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_and_Child "Virgin and Child")).

In 1865–67 a beacon was installed on the southeast terrace of the building and a telegraph service was started, while nearby a gas factory was built, producing smoke that prompted many protests.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11) The first moves to preserve and rehabilitate the tower began in the latter part of the 20th century. First, the tower was transferred to the [Ministry of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Finance_(Portugal) "Ministry of Finance (Portugal)") in 1940, which undertook small conservation works.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11) Then the military quarters on the battlements were removed and the inner [cloister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloister "Cloister") was built. The architectural landscape designer António Viana Barreto began a three-year project in 1953 to integrate the tower with the local shoreline.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11) In 1983 the site hosted the 17th European Exhibition on Art, Science and Culture, and various projects involving the building were undertaken, among them covering the cloister with a transparent plastic cupola. In the same year, the Belém Tower was classified by [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO") as a [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site").

In the 1990s, the property was transferred to the _Instituto Português do Património Arquitectónico_ (forerunner of [IGESPAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGESPAR "IGESPAR")), which began a full restoration of the building that lasted from February 1997 to January 1998; this included reinforcing the tower and bastion, reinforcing the south balcony supports with stainless steel rods and [epoxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epoxy "Epoxy") resin, treating the mortar joints, and general structural cleaning. The statues of Saint [Vincent of Saragossa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_of_Saragossa "Vincent of Saragossa") and the [Archangel Michael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_(archangel) "Michael (archangel)") received the same treatment.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-19) In 1999 the project received the _[Europa Nostra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa\_Nostra "Europa Nostra")_ award for its restoration of the exterior.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR_Tower-15) The Belém Tower was added on 7 July 2007 to the registry of the [Seven Wonders of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Wonders_of_Portugal "Seven Wonders of Portugal").

## Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bel%C3%A9m_Tower&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Architecture")]

The Belém Tower is situated on the northern bank of the [Tagus River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus_River "Tagus River") in the civil parish of [Santa Maria de Belém](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Maria_de_Bel%C3%A9m "Santa Maria de Belém"), municipality of Lisbon, accessible at the western end of the _Avenida de Brasília_ by a small bridge. Nearby are the [Jeronimos Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeronimos_Monastery "Jeronimos Monastery") to the east and the _Forte do Bom Sucesso_ to the west, while to the north are the tower Governor's residence, the old Governor's residence for the Bom Successo fort, and the Chapel of São Jerónimo.

The tower is isolated along the riverbank, between the dock of Bom Sucesso and Pedrouços, on a basaltic outcropping of rocks belonging to the geomorphological volcanic complex of Lisboa-Mafra.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Pais2011-20) Although various guides have claimed that the tower was built in the middle of the Tagus, and now sits near the shore after the [1755 earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake "1755 Lisbon earthquake") redirected the river, they are incorrect. The Portuguese [Ministry of Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Culture_(Portugal) "Ministry of Culture (Portugal)") and the [Institute of Architectural Heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGESPAR "IGESPAR") indicate that the tower was constructed on a small island near the bank of the Tagus, opposite the shore of Restelo. As development extended the shoreline progressively, more and more of the northern bank crept southwards into the Tagus, the tower becoming integrated into the riverbank over time.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Portugal_tourism-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR-8)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Rough_Guides-21)

The Belém Tower was built from a beige-white [limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone "Limestone") local to the Lisbon area and thereabouts called _Lioz_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Assembly2007-22) The building is divided into two parts: the [bastion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion "Bastion") and the four-story tower located on the north side of the bastion.

The 16th-century tower is considered one of the principal works of the [Portuguese Late Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture_of_Portugal#Manueline_style_(c._1490_%E2%80%93_c._1520) "Architecture of Portugal")[Manueline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manueline "Manueline") style.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Lach-4)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Rough_Guides-21) This is especially apparent in its elaborate [rib vaulting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rib_vault "Rib vault"), crosses of the [Order of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Christ_(Portugal) "Order of Christ (Portugal)"), [armillary spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armillary_sphere "Armillary sphere") and twisted rope, common to the nautically inspired organic Manueline style.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Lach-4)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR-8)

### Exterior

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bel%C3%A9m_Tower&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Exterior")]

[![Image 10: A detailed view of a turret. A cross sits atop each turret. Two Order of Christ crosses can be seen on the edge of the bastion.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Tour_de_Belem_detail_1_082006.JPG/250px-Tour_de_Belem_detail_1_082006.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tour_de_Belem_detail_1_082006.JPG)

Bastion terrace with its [Moorish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorish_architecture "Moorish architecture") bartizan [turrets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turret_(architecture) "Turret (architecture)") and cupolas from the northwest.

[![Image 11: The inner cloister and the back side of the virgin niche. In the centre is the opening into the casemate and in the background are two turrets on the bastion deck.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Belem.Torre04.jpg/250px-Belem.Torre04.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Belem.Torre04.jpg)

The inner [cloister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloister "Cloister") of the tower displaying the back side of the niche of the virgin and two turrets

The building's plan consists of a rectangular tower and an irregular, hexagonal bastion, with elongated flanks, that projects south into the river. It is basically a large articulated vertical space resting on a horizontal stone slab, covered by masonry enclosures. On the northeast angle of the structure, protected by a defensive wall with [bartizans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartizan "Bartizan"), is a drawbridge to access the bulwark, decorated in plant motifs, surmounted by the royal coat of arms and flanked by small columns, complemented with [armillary spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armillary_sphere "Armillary sphere"). The Manueline armillary spheres appear at the tower's entrance, symbolizing Portugal's [nautical explorations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Portugal_(1415%E2%80%931542) "History of Portugal (1415–1542)"), and were used on King Manuel I's personal banner to represent Portuguese discoveries during his rule.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR-8)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-manuelsphere-24) The decorative carved, twisted rope and elegant knots also point to Portugal's nautical history and are common elements of the Manueline style.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Lach-4)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR-8)

On the outside of the lower bastion, the walls have spaces for 17 cannons with [embrasures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embrasure "Embrasure") affording a view of the river.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Publishing2012-25) The upper tier of the bastion is crowned by a small wall with bartizans in strategic places, decorated by rounded shields with the cross of the Order of Christ encircling the platform. King [Manuel I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_I_of_Portugal "Manuel I of Portugal") was a member of the Order of Christ,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Knights-26) thus the cross of the [Order of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Christ_(Portugal) "Order of Christ (Portugal)") is used numerous times on the [parapets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parapet "Parapet").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-UNESCO2019-3)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR-8) These were a symbol of Manuel's military power, as the knights of the Order of Christ participated in several military conquests in that era.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Knights-26) The bartizans, cylindrical turrets ([guerites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerite "Guerite")) in the corners that served as watchtowers, have corbels with zoomorphic ornaments and domes covered with ridges unusual in European architecture, topped with ornate [finials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finial "Finial"). The bases of the turrets have images of beasts, including a rhinoceros.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Portugal_tourism-5)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Torre-17) This rhinoceros is considered to be the first sculpture of such an animal in Western European art[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Portugal_tourism-5) and probably depicts [the rhinoceros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BCrer's_Rhinoceros "Dürer's Rhinoceros") that Manuel I sent to [Pope Leo X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Leo_X "Pope Leo X") in 1515.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-RookmaakerJones1998-27)

While the tower is predominantly Manueline in style,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Lach-4) it also incorporates features of other architectural styles.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Portugal_tourism-5) It was built by the military architect Francisco de Arruda, who had already supervised the construction of several fortresses in Portuguese territories in [Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Almeida1992-13)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Torre-17) The influence of [Moorish architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorish_architecture "Moorish architecture") is manifested in the delicate decorations, the arched windows, the balconies, and the ribbed [cupolas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupola_(military) "Cupola (military)") of the [watchtowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watchtower "Watchtower").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-UNESCO2019-3)

The tower has four storeys, with fenestrations and battlements, the ground floor being occupied by a vaulted cistern. On the first floor, there is a south-facing rectangular door with arched windows on the east and north, and bartizans in the northeast and northwest corners. The southern part of the second floor is dominated by a covered veranda with a [loggia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loggia "Loggia") (_matacães_), consisting of an arcade of seven arches, resting on large [corbels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corbel "Corbel") with balusters. It is covered by laced stonework to form a porch, and its sloped roof ends in a sculpted twisted rope.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Watson-7) The eastern, northern and western walls are occupied by double-arched enclosures, with the northeast and northwest corners occupied by statues of Saint [Vincent of Saragossa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_of_Saragossa "Vincent of Saragossa") and the [archangel Michael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_(archangel) "Michael (archangel)") in niches. The third floor has twin windows in the northern, eastern and western façades, with balusters, interspersed by two armillary spheres and a large relief with the Royal coat of arms. The final floor is encircled by a terrace with shields of the Order of Christ, and a northern arched door and eastern arched window. The terrace is enclosed by a low wall with [colonnaded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonnade "Colonnade") pyramidal [merlons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merlon "Merlon") with [bartizans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartizan "Bartizan") in the four corners. A similar terrace above this floor offers a view of the surrounding landscape.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Sullivan-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-29)

### Interior

The interior of the bastion, with a circular staircase at the north end, has two contiguous halls with vaulted ceilings supported by masonry arches, as well as four storage lockers and sanitary facilities. On the ground floor bunker, the floor is inclined towards the outside, while the ceilings are supported by masonry pilasters and vaulted spines. Gothic rib vaulting is evident in this [casemate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casemate "Casemate"),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Bulwark-30) the rooms of the tower[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-31) and the cupolas of the [watchtowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watchtowers "Watchtowers") on the bastion terrace.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-UNESCO2019-3) Peripheral compartments on the edges of the bunker allow the individual cannons to occupy their own space, with the ceiling designed with several asymmetrical domes of various heights. The ancillary storerooms were later used as prison cells.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Bulwark_Terrace-32)

Two archways open to the main cloister in the north and south, while six broken arches stretch along the eastern and western parts of the cloister, interspersed with square pillars in the bastion interior, with gargoyle facets. The open cloister above the casemate, although decorative, was designed to dispel cannon smoke.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Torre-17)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Bulwark-30) The upper level is connected by a railing decorated with crosses of the Order of Christ, while at the terrace the space has rising columns topped with armillary spheres. This space could also be used for light-calibre infantry. This was the first Portuguese fortification with a two-level gun emplacement and marked a new development in military architecture. Some of the decorations date from the renovation of the 1840s and are [Neo-Manueline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Manueline "Neo-Manueline") in style, like the decoration of the small cloister on the bastion.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Torre-17)

On the southern portion of the cloister terrace is an image of the Virgin and Child. The statue of the Virgin of Belém also referred to as _Nossa Senhora de Bom Successo_ (Our Lady of Good Success), _Nossa Senhora das Uvas_ (Our Lady of the Grapes) or the _Virgem da Boa Viagem_ (Virgin of Safe Homecoming) is depicted holding a child in her right hand and a [bunch of grapes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunch_of_grapes "Bunch of grapes") in her left.

The tower is about 12 metres (39 ft) wide and 30 metres (98 ft) tall.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Watson-7) The first-floor interior contains the _Sala do Governador_ (Governor's Hall), an octagonal space that opens into the cistern, while in the northeast and northwest corners are corridors that link to the bartizans. A small door provides access via a spiral staircase to the subsequent floors. On the second floor, the _Sala dos Reis_ (King's Hall) opens to the [loggia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loggia "Loggia") overlooking the river, while a small corner fireplace extends from this floor to the third-floor fireplace in the _Sala das Audiências_ (Audience Hall). The ceilings of all three floors are covered in hollow concrete slabs. The fourth-floor chapel has a vaulted rib ceiling with niches emblematic of the Manueline style, supported by carved corbels.

**Belém Tower** (Portuguese: _Torre de Belém_, pronounced[[ˈtoʁɨ ðɨ βɨˈlɐ̃j]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Portuguese "Help:IPA/Portuguese"); literally: [Bethlehem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem "Bethlehem") Tower), officially the **Tower of [Saint Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_of_Saragossa "Vincent of Saragossa")** (Portuguese: _Torre de São Vicente_), is a 16th-century fortification located in [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), Portugal, which served as a point of embarkation and disembarkation for Portuguese explorers and as a ceremonial gateway to Lisbon.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-DHA-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-UNESCO2019-3) The tower symbolizes Portugal's maritime and colonial power in early modern Europe. It was built during the height of the [Portuguese Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Renaissance "Portuguese Renaissance") and is a prominent example of the Portuguese [Manueline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manueline "Manueline") style,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Lach-4) but it also incorporates other architectural styles, such as the minarets, which are inspired by [Moorish architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorish_architecture "Moorish architecture").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Portugal_tourism-5) The structure was built from [lioz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lioz "Lioz")[limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone "Limestone"), a material local to the Lisbon region,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-6) and is composed of a [bastion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion "Bastion") and a 30-metre (100 ft)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Watson-7) four-storey tower.

Since 1983, the tower has been a UNESCO [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site"), along with the [Jerónimos Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jer%C3%B3nimos_Monastery "Jerónimos Monastery"). It is often portrayed as a symbol of Europe's [Age of Discoveries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discoveries "Age of Discoveries")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-UNESCO2019-3) and as a metonym for [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal") or Lisbon, given its landmark status. It has incorrectly been stated that the tower was built in the middle of the Tagus and now sits near the shore because the river was redirected after the [1755 Lisbon earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake "1755 Lisbon earthquake"). In fact, the tower was built on a small island in the [Tagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus "Tagus") river near the Lisbon shore.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Portugal_tourism-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR-8)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bel%C3%A9m_Tower&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Lisbon_Torre_de_Bel%C3%A9m_BW_2018-10-03_16-34-03.jpg/250px-Lisbon_Torre_de_Bel%C3%A9m_BW_2018-10-03_16-34-03.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lisbon_Torre_de_Bel%C3%A9m_BW_2018-10-03_16-34-03.jpg)

The tower was classified as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983 and included in the registry of the [Seven Wonders of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Wonders_of_Portugal "Seven Wonders of Portugal") in 2007.

In the late 15th century, [King John II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_Portugal "John II of Portugal") had designed a defence system for the mouth of the Tagus that depended on the fortresses of [Cascais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cascais "Cascais") and _São Sebastião_ (or _Torre Velha_) in [Caparica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caparica_(Almada) "Caparica (Almada)") on the south side of the river.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Portugal_tourism-5)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBTorre-9) These fortresses did not completely protect the river's mouth, and further protection was required.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBTorre-9) In his "Chronicle of [John II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_Portugal "John II of Portugal")" (_Chronica de D. Joao II_), which appeared in 1545,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Hirsch1967-10) the author [Garcia de Resende](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garcia_de_Resende "Garcia de Resende") affirmed the king's opinion that the defences of Lisbon were inadequate, and that he had insisted on building fortifications along the entrance to the River [Tagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus "Tagus") to supplement the existing defences.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11) To this end, he ordered the "making of a strong fort", but died before any plans were drawn. King [Manuel I of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_I_of_Portugal "Manuel I of Portugal") revisited the proposal twenty years later and ordered the construction of a military fortification on the northern margin of the Tagus at Belém.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBTorre-9) In 1513, Lourenço Fernandes wrote a letter to his friends referring to the king's intention of constructing a tower near Restelo Velho, having determined it to be essential.

The presence of this military element was also a celebration of the round trip of the Portuguese to India and a way of receiving the fleets that arrived at the mouth of the Tagus, glorifying the feat, as if it were a mimetic of what those who arrived could identify with what they had seen in the East. The best example is the carved rhinoceros, the result of an offer from an Indian ruler who offered it to King Dom Manuel. This Rhinoceros would be the same one that [Albrecht Dürer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albrecht_D%C3%BCrer "Albrecht Dürer") would immortalize in his drawings.

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Portuguese_India_16-17th_centuries_v05.jpg/330px-Portuguese_India_16-17th_centuries_v05.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portuguese_India_16-17th_centuries_v05.jpg)

Portuguese presence in India, the Gulf of Bengal and the Himalayas (maximum extent) between the 15th and 17th centuries

The project was started on a basaltic rock outcrop a short distance from the riverbank, using some of the stone being collected to build the [Monastery of Santa Maria de Belém](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jer%C3%B3nimos_Monastery "Jerónimos Monastery"). The tower was designed by military architect [Francisco de Arruda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_de_Arruda "Francisco de Arruda"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Hourihane2012-12) named "Master of the works of the Belém stronghold" by King Manuel,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Almeida1992-13) and in 1516 he began receiving 763 blocks and 504 stones for its construction, delivered by Diogo Rodrigues, treasurer for the project. As construction progressed, a man-of-war called the _Grande Nau_ (Great Ship), a heavily armed, 1000–ton ship continued to guard the estuary at the mouth of the Tagus until the fort's completion.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR_Tower-15)

The building was finished in 1519, just two years before Manuel's death, and Gaspar de Paiva was temporarily stationed to command the fortress;[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-16) his commission was made permanent on 15 September 1521, when he was appointed the first Captain-General, or [alcalde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcalde "Alcalde"), and the fortress was named the Castle of St Vincent (_Castelo de São Vicente de Belém_),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Torre-17) in honour of the patron saint of Lisbon.

In 1571, [Francisco de Holanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_de_Holanda "Francisco de Holanda") advised the monarch that it was necessary to improve the coastal defences in order to protect the kingdom's capital. He suggested the construction of a "strong and impregnable" fort that could easily defend Lisbon and that the Belém Tower "should be strengthened, repaired and completed...that it has cost so much without being completed". D'Holanda designed an improved rectangular bastion with several turrets. In 1580, after a few hours of battle, the garrison stationed in the tower surrendered to Spanish forces under the command of the [Duke of Alba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fadrique_%C3%81lvarez_de_Toledo,_4th_Duke_of_Alba "Fadrique Álvarez de Toledo, 4th Duke of Alba"). After this defeat, the dungeons of the tower served as a prison until 1830.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Torre-17) It was also during the last quarter of the 16th century that the construction of the Philippine Barracks began. A rectangular two-storey space was constructed over the bastion, giving the tower the visual profile that it has retained to the present, with sculpted crosses of the [Order of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Christ_(Portugal) "Order of Christ (Portugal)") and domed turrets.

In 1589, [Philip I of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_I_of_Portugal "Philip I of Portugal") ordered Italian engineer Friar João Vicenzio Casale to build a well-defended fort to be constructed in place of the "useless castle of São Vicente".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11) The engineer submitted three designs, proposing that the bastion would be surrounded by another bastion of greater dimensions, but the project never materialized.

A 1633 codex for the House of Cadaval was inserted into one of the floors, in one of the arches of the barracks, and in the four largest arches at the top of the southern façade. Similarly, a reference to the year 1655 was inscribed on a plaque placed on the northern wall of the cloister, which certified the tower's function as a customs control point and for navigation along the Tagus; vessels were obliged to pay a tax as they entered the harbour, which was imposed incrementally.

Between 1780 and 1782, under the reign of [Maria I of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_I_of_Portugal "Maria I of Portugal"), General Guilherme de Valleré constructed the [Fort of Bom Sucesso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_of_Bom_Sucesso "Fort of Bom Sucesso"), whose battery was connected by a western corridor wall to the tower.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11) When French forces invaded Lisbon during the [Peninsular War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peninsular_War "Peninsular War"), detachments of their troops were quartered in the tower from 1808 to 1814. After the French retreated, [Lord Beresford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Beresford,_1st_Viscount_Beresford "William Beresford, 1st Viscount Beresford") advised that coastal artillery batteries should be reinforced along the Tagus, and specifically noted that stronger batteries should be placed on the sides of the tower's bastion, with carts placed to better protect the soldiers, since the walls were very low.

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Combat_du_Tage.jpg/250px-Combat_du_Tage.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Combat_du_Tage.jpg)

French ships exchanging fire with the tower during the [Battle of the Tagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Tagus_(1831) "Battle of the Tagus (1831)") of the [Liberal Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Wars "Liberal Wars")

[King Miguel I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_of_Portugal "Miguel of Portugal") (1828–1834) used the dungeons to imprison his liberal opponents,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Watson-7) while another level was used as a [custom house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Custom_house "Custom house") for ships until the duty on foreign ships was abolished in 1833.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Torre-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Penny-18) The tower received military upgrades in 1589 and 1809–1814.

During the reign of [Maria II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_II_of_Portugal "Maria II of Portugal"), [Almeida Garrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almeida_Garrett "Almeida Garrett") protested the site's degradation and under the persuasion of the [Duke of Terceira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_Jos%C3%A9_Severim_de_Noronha,_1st_Duke_of_Terceira "António José Severim de Noronha, 1st Duke of Terceira"), renovations were begun by military engineer António de Azevedo e Cunha.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11) He demolished the Philippine barracks and extended revivalist elements in 1845–46 (such as the armoured merlons, the [balustrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baluster "Baluster") of the veranda along the southern façade, the laced fascia in the cloister and the niche with an image of the [Virgin and Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_and_Child "Virgin and Child")).

In 1865–67 a beacon was installed on the southeast terrace of the building and a telegraph service was started, while nearby a gas factory was built, producing smoke that prompted many protests.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11) The first moves to preserve and rehabilitate the tower began in the latter part of the 20th century. First, the tower was transferred to the [Ministry of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Finance_(Portugal) "Ministry of Finance (Portugal)") in 1940, which undertook small conservation works.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11) Then the military quarters on the battlements were removed and the inner [cloister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloister "Cloister") was built. The architectural landscape designer António Viana Barreto began a three-year project in 1953 to integrate the tower with the local shoreline.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-TBHistoria-11) In 1983 the site hosted the 17th European Exhibition on Art, Science and Culture, and various projects involving the building were undertaken, among them covering the cloister with a transparent plastic cupola. In the same year, the Belém Tower was classified by [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO") as a [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site").

In the 1990s, the property was transferred to the _Instituto Português do Património Arquitectónico_ (forerunner of [IGESPAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGESPAR "IGESPAR")), which began a full restoration of the building that lasted from February 1997 to January 1998; this included reinforcing the tower and bastion, reinforcing the south balcony supports with stainless steel rods and [epoxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epoxy "Epoxy") resin, treating the mortar joints, and general structural cleaning. The statues of Saint [Vincent of Saragossa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_of_Saragossa "Vincent of Saragossa") and the [Archangel Michael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_(archangel) "Michael (archangel)") received the same treatment.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-19) In 1999 the project received the _[Europa Nostra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa\_Nostra "Europa Nostra")_ award for its restoration of the exterior.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR_Tower-15) The Belém Tower was added on 7 July 2007 to the registry of the [Seven Wonders of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Wonders_of_Portugal "Seven Wonders of Portugal").

## Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bel%C3%A9m_Tower&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Architecture")]

The Belém Tower is situated on the northern bank of the [Tagus River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagus_River "Tagus River") in the civil parish of [Santa Maria de Belém](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Maria_de_Bel%C3%A9m "Santa Maria de Belém"), municipality of Lisbon, accessible at the western end of the _Avenida de Brasília_ by a small bridge. Nearby are the [Jeronimos Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeronimos_Monastery "Jeronimos Monastery") to the east and the _Forte do Bom Sucesso_ to the west, while to the north are the tower Governor's residence, the old Governor's residence for the Bom Successo fort, and the Chapel of São Jerónimo.

The tower is isolated along the riverbank, between the dock of Bom Sucesso and Pedrouços, on a basaltic outcropping of rocks belonging to the geomorphological volcanic complex of Lisboa-Mafra.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Pais2011-20) Although various guides have claimed that the tower was built in the middle of the Tagus, and now sits near the shore after the [1755 earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake "1755 Lisbon earthquake") redirected the river, they are incorrect. The Portuguese [Ministry of Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Culture_(Portugal) "Ministry of Culture (Portugal)") and the [Institute of Architectural Heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGESPAR "IGESPAR") indicate that the tower was constructed on a small island near the bank of the Tagus, opposite the shore of Restelo. As development extended the shoreline progressively, more and more of the northern bank crept southwards into the Tagus, the tower becoming integrated into the riverbank over time.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Portugal_tourism-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR-8)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Rough_Guides-21)

The Belém Tower was built from a beige-white [limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone "Limestone") local to the Lisbon area and thereabouts called _Lioz_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Assembly2007-22) The building is divided into two parts: the [bastion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion "Bastion") and the four-story tower located on the north side of the bastion.

The 16th-century tower is considered one of the principal works of the [Portuguese Late Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture_of_Portugal#Manueline_style_(c._1490_%E2%80%93_c._1520) "Architecture of Portugal")[Manueline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manueline "Manueline") style.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Lach-4)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Rough_Guides-21) This is especially apparent in its elaborate [rib vaulting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rib_vault "Rib vault"), crosses of the [Order of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Christ_(Portugal) "Order of Christ (Portugal)"), [armillary spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armillary_sphere "Armillary sphere") and twisted rope, common to the nautically inspired organic Manueline style.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Lach-4)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR-8)

### Exterior

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bel%C3%A9m_Tower&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Exterior")]

[![Image 10: A detailed view of a turret. A cross sits atop each turret. Two Order of Christ crosses can be seen on the edge of the bastion.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Tour_de_Belem_detail_1_082006.JPG/250px-Tour_de_Belem_detail_1_082006.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tour_de_Belem_detail_1_082006.JPG)

Bastion terrace with its [Moorish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorish_architecture "Moorish architecture") bartizan [turrets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turret_(architecture) "Turret (architecture)") and cupolas from the northwest.

[![Image 11: The inner cloister and the back side of the virgin niche. In the centre is the opening into the casemate and in the background are two turrets on the bastion deck.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Belem.Torre04.jpg/250px-Belem.Torre04.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Belem.Torre04.jpg)

The inner [cloister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloister "Cloister") of the tower displaying the back side of the niche of the virgin and two turrets

The building's plan consists of a rectangular tower and an irregular, hexagonal bastion, with elongated flanks, that projects south into the river. It is basically a large articulated vertical space resting on a horizontal stone slab, covered by masonry enclosures. On the northeast angle of the structure, protected by a defensive wall with [bartizans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartizan "Bartizan"), is a drawbridge to access the bulwark, decorated in plant motifs, surmounted by the royal coat of arms and flanked by small columns, complemented with [armillary spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armillary_sphere "Armillary sphere"). The Manueline armillary spheres appear at the tower's entrance, symbolizing Portugal's [nautical explorations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Portugal_(1415%E2%80%931542) "History of Portugal (1415–1542)"), and were used on King Manuel I's personal banner to represent Portuguese discoveries during his rule.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR-8)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-manuelsphere-24) The decorative carved, twisted rope and elegant knots also point to Portugal's nautical history and are common elements of the Manueline style.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Lach-4)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR-8)

On the outside of the lower bastion, the walls have spaces for 17 cannons with [embrasures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embrasure "Embrasure") affording a view of the river.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Publishing2012-25) The upper tier of the bastion is crowned by a small wall with bartizans in strategic places, decorated by rounded shields with the cross of the Order of Christ encircling the platform. King [Manuel I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_I_of_Portugal "Manuel I of Portugal") was a member of the Order of Christ,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Knights-26) thus the cross of the [Order of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Christ_(Portugal) "Order of Christ (Portugal)") is used numerous times on the [parapets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parapet "Parapet").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-UNESCO2019-3)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-IPPAR-8) These were a symbol of Manuel's military power, as the knights of the Order of Christ participated in several military conquests in that era.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Knights-26) The bartizans, cylindrical turrets ([guerites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerite "Guerite")) in the corners that served as watchtowers, have corbels with zoomorphic ornaments and domes covered with ridges unusual in European architecture, topped with ornate [finials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finial "Finial"). The bases of the turrets have images of beasts, including a rhinoceros.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Portugal_tourism-5)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Torre-17) This rhinoceros is considered to be the first sculpture of such an animal in Western European art[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Portugal_tourism-5) and probably depicts [the rhinoceros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BCrer's_Rhinoceros "Dürer's Rhinoceros") that Manuel I sent to [Pope Leo X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Leo_X "Pope Leo X") in 1515.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-RookmaakerJones1998-27)

While the tower is predominantly Manueline in style,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Lach-4) it also incorporates features of other architectural styles.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Portugal_tourism-5) It was built by the military architect Francisco de Arruda, who had already supervised the construction of several fortresses in Portuguese territories in [Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Almeida1992-13)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Torre-17) The influence of [Moorish architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorish_architecture "Moorish architecture") is manifested in the delicate decorations, the arched windows, the balconies, and the ribbed [cupolas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupola_(military) "Cupola (military)") of the [watchtowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watchtower "Watchtower").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-UNESCO2019-3)

The tower has four storeys, with fenestrations and battlements, the ground floor being occupied by a vaulted cistern. On the first floor, there is a south-facing rectangular door with arched windows on the east and north, and bartizans in the northeast and northwest corners. The southern part of the second floor is dominated by a covered veranda with a [loggia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loggia "Loggia") (_matacães_), consisting of an arcade of seven arches, resting on large [corbels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corbel "Corbel") with balusters. It is covered by laced stonework to form a porch, and its sloped roof ends in a sculpted twisted rope.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Watson-7) The eastern, northern and western walls are occupied by double-arched enclosures, with the northeast and northwest corners occupied by statues of Saint [Vincent of Saragossa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_of_Saragossa "Vincent of Saragossa") and the [archangel Michael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_(archangel) "Michael (archangel)") in niches. The third floor has twin windows in the northern, eastern and western façades, with balusters, interspersed by two armillary spheres and a large relief with the Royal coat of arms. The final floor is encircled by a terrace with shields of the Order of Christ, and a northern arched door and eastern arched window. The terrace is enclosed by a low wall with [colonnaded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonnade "Colonnade") pyramidal [merlons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merlon "Merlon") with [bartizans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartizan "Bartizan") in the four corners. A similar terrace above this floor offers a view of the surrounding landscape.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Sullivan-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-29)

### Interior

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bel%C3%A9m_Tower&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Interior")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Belem.Torre09.jpg/250px-Belem.Torre09.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Belem.Torre09.jpg)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/Lisbon_holiday_%2818798806522%29.jpg/250px-Lisbon_holiday_%2818798806522%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lisbon_holiday_(18798806522).jpg)

Tourists visiting inside

The interior of the bastion, with a circular staircase at the north end, has two contiguous halls with vaulted ceilings supported by masonry arches, as well as four storage lockers and sanitary facilities. On the ground floor bunker, the floor is inclined towards the outside, while the ceilings are supported by masonry pilasters and vaulted spines. Gothic rib vaulting is evident in this [casemate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casemate "Casemate"),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Bulwark-30) the rooms of the tower[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-31) and the cupolas of the [watchtowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watchtowers "Watchtowers") on the bastion terrace.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-UNESCO2019-3) Peripheral compartments on the edges of the bunker allow the individual cannons to occupy their own space, with the ceiling designed with several asymmetrical domes of various heights. The ancillary storerooms were later used as prison cells.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Bulwark_Terrace-32)

Two archways open to the main cloister in the north and south, while six broken arches stretch along the eastern and western parts of the cloister, interspersed with square pillars in the bastion interior, with gargoyle facets. The open cloister above the casemate, although decorative, was designed to dispel cannon smoke.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Torre-17)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Bulwark-30) The upper level is connected by a railing decorated with crosses of the Order of Christ, while at the terrace the space has rising columns topped with armillary spheres. This space could also be used for light-calibre infantry. This was the first Portuguese fortification with a two-level gun emplacement and marked a new development in military architecture. Some of the decorations date from the renovation of the 1840s and are [Neo-Manueline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Manueline "Neo-Manueline") in style, like the decoration of the small cloister on the bastion.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Torre-17)

On the southern portion of the cloister terrace is an image of the Virgin and Child. The statue of the Virgin of Belém also referred to as _Nossa Senhora de Bom Successo_ (Our Lady of Good Success), _Nossa Senhora das Uvas_ (Our Lady of the Grapes) or the _Virgem da Boa Viagem_ (Virgin of Safe Homecoming) is depicted holding a child in her right hand and a [bunch of grapes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunch_of_grapes "Bunch of grapes") in her left.

The tower is about 12 metres (39 ft) wide and 30 metres (98 ft) tall.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Tower#cite_note-Watson-7) The first-floor interior contains the _Sala do Governador_ (Governor's Hall), an octagonal space that opens into the cistern, while in the northeast and northwest corners are corridors that link to the bartizans. A small door provides access via a spiral staircase to the subsequent floors. On the second floor, the _Sala dos Reis_ (King's Hall) opens to the [loggia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loggia "Loggia") overlooking the river, while a small corner fireplace extends from this floor to the third-floor fireplace in the _Sala das Audiências_ (Audience Hall). The ceilings of all three floors are covered in hollow concrete slabs. The fourth-floor chapel has a vaulted rib ceiling with niches emblematic of the Manueline style, supported by carved corbels.

# Monument of the Discoveries

Site:Padrão dos Descobrimentos, Portugal Student/Author:Chaney Fix ’26![Image 1: Monument of the Discoveries. Carved figures are ascending a ramp. All of this is artistically rendered in stone.](https://nanovic.nd.edu/assets/593184/header.jpg)
## Background

The Monument of the Discoveries, or Padrão dos Descobrimentos, stands 170 feet tall along the picturesque bank of the Tagus River in Lisbon, Portugal. Located in the Santa Maria de Belém area, the site commemorates prominent historical figures from the 15th and 16th century Portuguese Age of Discovery. The monument was originally constructed for the 1940 Portuguese World Exhibition as a temporary exhibit to celebrate Portugal’s maritime prowess and national pride. Originally constructed out of perishable materials, the statue was reconstructed in 1960 in honor of the fifth centenary of Prince Henry the Navigator, the monument’s forefront figure. The figures behind Henry represent important Portuguese leaders that succeeded Henry’s time, including monarchs, explorers, scientists, and missionaries. Some of the most renowned include Vasco de Gama, Pedro Álvares Cabral, and Ferdinand Magellan. The monument was rebuilt using cement and rose-colored stone, with limestone figures.

The design of the structure is meant to invoke the prow of a caravel, a Portuguese sailing ship instrumental during Portuguese exploration, while the entrance resembles a sword, a symbol of the Portuguese military and strength. In front of the monument sits an enormous pavement featuring a map of Portuguese voyages, crafted in traditional Portuguese patterns of multi-colored limestone and marble. This map serves as a visual representation of Portugal’s extensive maritime explorations and conquests. It can be viewed best from the overlook located at the top of the monument.

![Image 2: Monument of the Discoveries. This view of the monument shows a high protruding, prow-like structure evocative of a naval vessel.](https://nanovic.nd.edu/assets/593189/fullsize/grid_l.jpg)

![Image 3: Monument of the Discoveries. Carved figures are ascending a ramp. All of this is artistically rendered in stone.](https://nanovic.nd.edu/assets/593190/fullsize/grid_r.jpg)

## Analysis

The Monument of the Discoveries is more than a tribute, but rather a statement of Portuguese power and influence. The large figures scaling the sides of the structure, combined with the imposing sword-like entrance and caravel design, emphasize this extensive naval power. However, it is critical to remember that this power came at the expense of other nations and cultures, reflecting a complex and controversial legacy. The so-called “Age of Discovery” was a period during which the Portuguese empire came into contact with other nations, frequently leading to their colonization. While the monument remains a powerful symbol of Portugal’s historical impact on global exploration, it should additionally prompt reflection on the broader consequences of imperialism and push modern-day Portugal to further reparations.

Today, the site is visited by large numbers of tourists throughout the year due to its grandiose appearance and placement between the historic Belém Tower and Jerónimos Monastery. Most visitors pay the entrance fee thinking that their tour will solely consist of a laborious climb up a few floors for a nice view of Belem, Lisbon, but they would be dismissing the museum on the bottom floor. While one might expect this museum to detail the history of the monument, it is dedicated to an entirely different story.

![Image 4: A museum inscription on a wall. The header reads "Photographic portraits fo the african diaspora before 1975. Aurora Almada e Santos."](https://nanovic.nd.edu/assets/593191/museum.jpg)
Titled “Family Albums, Photographs of the African Diaspora in Greater Lisbon (1975 to Today),” the bottom floor of the site contains various media depicting the community of African people and people of African origin living in the Lisbon area. This gallery is temporary, implemented as a part of the United Nations’ International Decade for People of African Descent (2015–2024). In collaboration with the UN’s recognition efforts, Portuguese cultural and historical societies are also celebrating the lives of the many black Portuguese people descended from Africans who lived under Portuguese colonial rule. The exhibit includes everything from vintage family photographs to televised interviews to modern-day TikTok posts by black Portuguese creators. Each piece of media is accompanied by a brief story, shared by the featured individuals or their family and friends. Despite the important contents of this exhibit, there is little to no promotional material outside or on the ground floor of the monument and thus the onus falls on museum staff to direct visitors downstairs.

The creation of this museum is particularly intriguing when considering its origins during the 1960s, a pivotal decade for African independence. During this period, many African nations achieved independence from European colonial powers, including 17 countries in 1960 alone. Following the end of the Portuguese Salazar regime in 1974 and the dissolution of colonial rule, Angola, Mozambique, Guinea-Bissau, and Cape Verde all gained independence from Portugal by the end of 1975. This development led to a significant influx of immigrants from these former colonies to Portugal, “over one million people – that is to say, an increase in the population of over 12.5 per cent” (Marques 2012, 128).

![Image 5: Photographs displayed in a museum exhibit.](https://nanovic.nd.edu/assets/593192/museum2.jpg)
In response to this demographic shift, “the post-revolutionary Portuguese government had made a pledge to achieve decolonization” and “to accommodate the sudden demographic outburst resulting from those who decided to settle” (Marques 2012, 130). Measures included providing welfare, emergency housing, employment, and documentation. Alongside these efforts, a broader cultural renaissance emerged, with a resurgence of previously suppressed traditions and a rise in African identity across various nations, reflecting the growth of Pan-Africanism and a sense of unity among African countries. The “Family Albums” museum celebrates this rich heritage and the identity of African people and their descendants living in Portugal today. It highlights the beauty and significance of their family heritage and traditions, honoring the legacy and continuity of their cultural contributions over time.

The Monument of the Discoveries remains one of the most visited sites in Portugal today and likely will remain so for many generations to come. The impressive design and scale of the site, as well as recognizable figures, inspire visitors to delve deeper into the profound impact that Portugal’s naval and military might had on global exploration during the Age of Exploration. Today, the monument attracts visitors eager to appreciate its historical significance and scenic views of Lisbon, but it also houses the “Family Albums” contemporary exhibit. This exhibit, while temporary, makes an effort to highlight the often-overlooked consequences of colonialism on other nations and cultures. This gallery shifts the focus from the past to the present while acknowledging and celebrating the rich and diverse contributions of its African communities. At the conclusion of this temporary exhibition, it can only be hoped that the monument will fill the space so that it both celebrates and critically examines Portugal’s complex history, encouraging ongoing dialogue and reflection.

![Image 6: Exterior aerial view of the plaza in front the Monument of the Discoveries structure.](https://nanovic.nd.edu/assets/593193/fullsize/exterior.jpg)
