**Lüderitz** is a town in the [ǁKaras Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C7%81Karas_Region "ǁKaras Region") of southern [Namibia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namibia "Namibia"). It lies on one of the least hospitable coasts in Africa. It is a port developed around Robert Harbour and [Shark Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shark_Island,_Namibia "Shark Island, Namibia"). Lüderitz had a population of 16,125 people in 2023.

The town is known for its [colonial architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_architecture "Colonial architecture"), including some [Art Nouveau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Nouveau "Art Nouveau") work, and wildlife, including [seals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_(mammal) "Seal (mammal)"), [penguins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin "Penguin"), [flamingos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamingo "Flamingo"), and [ostriches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrich "Ostrich"). It is also home to a museum and lies at the end of a currently[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=L%C3%BCderitz&action=edit) decommissioned [railway line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_line "Railway line") to [Keetmanshoop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keetmanshoop "Keetmanshoop"). The town is named after [Adolf Lüderitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_L%C3%BCderitz "Adolf Lüderitz"), founder of the [German South West Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_South_West_Africa "German South West Africa") colony.

## Economy and infrastructure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=L%C3%BCderitz&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Economy and infrastructure")]

The centre of Lüderitz's economic activity is the port, until the incorporation of the [Walvis Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walvis_Bay "Walvis Bay")[exclave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exclave "Exclave") in 1994, the only suitable harbour on Namibia's coast. However, the harbour at Lüderitz has a comparatively shallow rock bottom, making it unusable for many modern ships. The recent addition of a new [quay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quay "Quay") has allowed larger fishing vessels to dock at Lüderitz. The town has also re-styled itself in an attempt to lure tourists to the area, which includes a new [waterfront](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterfront_(area) "Waterfront (area)") area for shops and offices.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") magazine _[Der Spiegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der\_Spiegel "Der Spiegel")_ reports that a massive [green hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_hydrogen "Green hydrogen") project is taking shape 80 kilometres south of Lüderitz, in [Tsau ǁKhaeb Sperrgebiet National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsau_%C7%81Khaeb_Sperrgebiet_National_Park "Tsau ǁKhaeb Sperrgebiet National Park"). For the operation of one of the five largest hydrogen plants in the world, 500 wind turbines and 40 square kilometres of solar panels are to be constructed. The green hydrogen will be piped to Lüderitz, where a desalination plant and an ammonia production facility are planned. The total investment will roughly equal Namibia's entire gross domestic product.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-2)

Lüderitz is situated on the [B4 national road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B4_road_(Namibia) "B4 road (Namibia)") to [Keetmanshoop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keetmanshoop "Keetmanshoop"). It is also the terminus of the 318 kilometres (198 mi) railway line to [Seeheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seeheim "Seeheim"), where the railway connects to the rest of the country's network. This line, built by inmates of the concentration camp on Shark Island, was completed in 1908[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-KDRail-3) but is currently not operational. Rebuilding of the remaining 47 kilometres (29 mi) track gap to [Aus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aus,_Namibia "Aus, Namibia") has been delayed since 2009.

The town very early had a power plant, used to power the electrified railway lines that served the diamond mining industry in Kolmanskop, [Pomona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomona,_Namibia "Pomona, Namibia"), [Bogenfels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogenfels "Bogenfels") (completed 1913), and [Charlottental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlottental?action=edit&redlink=1 "Charlottental (page does not exist)") (completed 1920). With 1.5 megawatts (2,000 hp) of output, it is assumed to be the largest in Africa at that time.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-history2-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-Eisenbahn-5)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=L%C3%BCderitz&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/L%C3%BCderitz_Territory_%28formerly_Angra_Pequena%29%2C_today_L%C3%BCderitz%2C_Namibia_German_Medal_1884%2C_obverse.jpg/250px-L%C3%BCderitz_Territory_%28formerly_Angra_Pequena%29%2C_today_L%C3%BCderitz%2C_Namibia_German_Medal_1884%2C_obverse.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:L%C3%BCderitz_Territory_(formerly_Angra_Pequena),_today_L%C3%BCderitz,_Namibia_German_Medal_1884,_obverse.jpg)

Angra Pequena View from Nautilus Point, German [Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal "Medal") 1884, obverse

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/L%C3%BCderitz_Territory_%28formerly_Angra_Pequena%29%2C_today_L%C3%BCderitz%2C_Namibia_German_Medal_1884%2C_reverse.jpg/250px-L%C3%BCderitz_Territory_%28formerly_Angra_Pequena%29%2C_today_L%C3%BCderitz%2C_Namibia_German_Medal_1884%2C_reverse.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:L%C3%BCderitz_Territory_(formerly_Angra_Pequena),_today_L%C3%BCderitz,_Namibia_German_Medal_1884,_reverse.jpg)

German Protectorate Medal [Lüderitz Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%BCderitz_Bay "Lüderitz Bay") 7 August 1884, reverse.

The bay on which Lüderitz is situated was first known to Europeans when [Bartolomeu Dias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolomeu_Dias "Bartolomeu Dias") encountered it in 1487. He named the bay _[Angra Pequena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angra\_Pequena "Angra Pequena")_ ([Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"): _Small Bay_) and erected a [padrão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padr%C3%A3o "Padrão") (stone cross) on the southern peninsula. In the 18th century, Dutch adventurers and scientists explored the area in search of minerals, but did not have much success. Further exploration expeditions followed in the early 19th century, during which the vast wildlife in the ocean was discovered. Profitable enterprises were set up, including [whaling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whaling "Whaling"), [seal hunting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_hunting "Seal hunting"), fishing, and [guano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guano "Guano")harvesting. Lüderitz thus began its life as a [trading post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trading_post "Trading post").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-L%C3%BCderitzbucht-6)

The town was founded in 1883 when Heinrich Vogelsang purchased Angra Pequena and some of the surrounding land on behalf of [Adolf Lüderitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_L%C3%BCderitz "Adolf Lüderitz"), a _[Hanseatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanseaten\_(class) "Hanseaten (class)")_ from [Bremen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bremen "Bremen") in [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), from the local [Nama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nama_people "Nama people") chief [Josef Frederiks II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josef_Frederiks_II "Josef Frederiks II") in [Bethanie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethanie,_Namibia "Bethanie, Namibia"). On 7 August 1884, the German Flag was officially hoisted in Angra Pequena. When Adolf Lüderitz did not return from an expedition to the [Orange River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_River "Orange River") in 1886, Angra Pequena was named _Lüderitzbucht_ in his honour.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-L%C3%BCderitzbucht-6) The later shortening of the town's name to _Lüderitz_ also refers to him.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-EB1911-7) In 1905, German authorities established a [concentration camp on Shark Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shark_Island_Concentration_Camp "Shark Island Concentration Camp"). The camp, access to which was very restricted, operated between 1905 and 1907 during the [Herero Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herero_Wars "Herero Wars"). Between 1,000 and 3,000 Africans from the [Herero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herero_people "Herero people") and Nama tribes died here as a result of the tragic conditions of forced labour. Their labour was used for the expansion of the city, railway, port, and on the farms of white settlers.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmererZeller200380-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErichsen2005[[Category:Wikipedia_articles_needing_page_number_citations_from_February_2013]]%3Csup_class=%22noprint_Inline-Template_%22_style=%22white-space:nowrap;%22%3E[%3Ci%3E[[Wikipedia:Citing_sources|%3Cspan_title=%22This_citation_requires_a_reference_to_the_specific_page_or_range_of_pages_in_which_the_material_appears.%20(February_2013)%22%3Epage%C2%A0needed%3C/span%3E]]%3C/i%3E]%3C/sup%3E-10)

In 1909, after the discovery of [diamonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond "Diamond") nearby, Lüderitz enjoyed a sudden surge of prosperity due to the development of a [diamond rush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond_rush "Diamond rush") to the area. In 1912, Lüderitz already had 1,100 inhabitants, not counting the indigenous population. Although situated in a harsh environment between desert and Ocean, trade in the harbour town surged, and the adjacent diamond mining settlement of [Kolmanskop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmanskop "Kolmanskop") was built.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-Gondwana-11)

After the German [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") capitulation, [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_South_Africa "Union of South Africa") took over the administration of [German South West Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_South_West_Africa "German South West Africa") in 1915. Many Germans were deported from Lüderitz, contributing to its shrinking population numbers. From 1920 onwards, diamond mining was only conducted further south of the town in places like [Pomona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomona,_Namibia "Pomona, Namibia") and [Elizabeth Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Bay,_Namibia "Elizabeth Bay, Namibia"). This development consequently led to the loss of Lüderitz's importance as a trading place. Only small fishing enterprises, minimal dock activity, and a few carpet weavers remained.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-Gondwana-11)

To remove colonial names from the maps of [Namibia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namibia "Namibia"), on 8 August 2013, the Namibian government renamed the constituency ǃNamiǂNûs, its name before 1884.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-13)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=L%C3%BCderitz&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Kolmanskop_near_L%C3%BCderitz%2C_Namibia_%282017%29.jpg/250px-Kolmanskop_near_L%C3%BCderitz%2C_Namibia_%282017%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kolmanskop_near_L%C3%BCderitz,_Namibia_(2017).jpg)

Ghost town [Kolmanskop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmanskop "Kolmanskop") (2017)

Just outside Lüderitz lies the [ghost town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_town "Ghost town") of [Kolmanskop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmanskop "Kolmanskop"), a prominent tourist destination in the [Namib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namib "Namib") Desert. This previously bustling diamond town is now abandoned and fights a constant struggle against being buried under the shifting [dunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dune "Dune") of the desert.

### Conservation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=L%C3%BCderitz&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Conservation")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Dolphins_at_L%C3%BCderitz%2C_Namibia_%283144863196%29.jpg/250px-Dolphins_at_L%C3%BCderitz%2C_Namibia_%283144863196%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dolphins_at_L%C3%BCderitz,_Namibia_(3144863196).jpg)

[Heaviside's dolphin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heaviside's_dolphin "Heaviside's dolphin") off Lüderitz.

The coastline of the area is recognised by [Bird Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BirdLife_International "BirdLife International") and other global conservation groups as being an [Important Bird Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Important_Bird_Area "Important Bird Area") (IBA), i.e., vital for coastal seabird breeding.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-15)

In April 2009, an [oil spill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_L%C3%BCderitz_oil_spill "2009 Lüderitz oil spill") from an [oil tanker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_tanker "Oil tanker") risked the safety of countless [African penguins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_penguin "African penguin") and numerous other species of endemic flora and fauna.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-16)

Several species of [cetacean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cetacea "Cetacea"), notably the diminutive [Heaviside's dolphin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heaviside's_dolphin "Heaviside's dolphin"), can be seen closer to shore; larger whales such as [southern right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_right_whale "Southern right whale"),[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-18)[humpback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale "Humpback whale"), [minke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minke_whale "Minke whale"), [fin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fin_whale "Fin whale"), and [pygmy right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pygmy_right_whale "Pygmy right whale") are found in [pelagic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelagic_zone "Pelagic zone") zones further from the mainland.

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=L%C3%BCderitz&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Climate")]

Lüderitz has a [cold desert climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_desert_climate "Cold desert climate") (_[BWk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BWk "BWk")_, according to the [Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification")), with cool to mild temperatures throughout the year and very little precipitation; average annual rainfall is just 17 millimetres (0.67 [inches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inch "Inch")). Windy, overcast and cold conditions can occur due to the cold [South Atlantic current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Atlantic_Current "South Atlantic Current") on the coast.

## Politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=L%C3%BCderitz&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Politics")]

Lüderitz is twinned with [Lüderitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%BCderitz,_Germany "Lüderitz, Germany") in Germany, part of the town of [Tangerhütte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangerh%C3%BCtte "Tangerhütte") since 2010.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-20)

Lüderitz is governed by a town council that has seven seats.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-22)

The [2015 local authority election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namibian_local_and_regional_elections,_2015 "Namibian local and regional elections, 2015") was won by [SWAPO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SWAPO "SWAPO"), which gained six seats (2,679 votes). The remaining seat went to the [Democratic Turnhalle Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Turnhalle_Alliance "Democratic Turnhalle Alliance") (DTA) with 265 votes.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-23) SWAPO also won the [2020 local authority election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Namibian_local_and_regional_elections "2020 Namibian local and regional elections") but lost majority control over the town council. SWAPO obtained 1,244 votes and gained three seats. [Independent Patriots for Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Patriots_for_Change "Independent Patriots for Change") (IPC), an opposition party formed in August 2020, gained 990 votes and two seats. One seat each went to the [Landless People's Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landless_People's_Movement_(Namibia) "Landless People's Movement (Namibia)") (LPM, a new party registered in 2018) with 515 votes and the [Popular Democratic Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Democratic_Movement "Popular Democratic Movement") (PDM, the new name of the DTA since 2017) with 343 votes.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-24)

## Culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=L%C3%BCderitz&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Culture")]

### Media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=L%C3%BCderitz&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Media")]

Lüderitz has a local monthly newspaper, _Buchter News_. The paper, which was started as a source of free English-language reading material, is run by volunteers from the British gap year charity Project Trust.

### Sport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=L%C3%BCderitz&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Sport")]

Lüderitz is home to the [Lüderitz Speed Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%BCderitz_Speed_Challenge "Lüderitz Speed Challenge"), the only international sporting event held in the town. This is an annual 6-week-long speed sailing event held in October and November each year under the auspices of the [International Sailing Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Sailing_Federation "International Sailing Federation") (ISAF) World Sailing Speed Record Council ([WSSRC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSSRC "WSSRC")).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-25) The Event is the brainchild of French kitesurfer Sebastian Cattalan, who became the first sailor in history to break the 50 Knot barrier in the purpose-built [canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canal "Canal") with a speed of 50.26 Knots in 2008.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-26)

In October 2011, Turkish-born American adventurer [Erden Eruç](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erden_Eru%C3%A7 "Erden Eruç") departed from Lüderitz Bay for the final ocean crossing of his Guinness world record-setting _solo_ human-powered [circumnavigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumnavigation "Circumnavigation") of the Earth.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-gwr-27) Eruç rowed to South America in an oceangoing rowboat, taking five months for the crossing to the town of [Güiria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCiria "Güiria"), [Venezuela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuela "Venezuela").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-psd-28)

*   **Deutsche Afrika Bank** building, erected in 1907, national monument[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-new-30)
*   **Felsenkirche** (English: Rock Church) on Diamond Hill, a church in [vertical Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_Revival_architecture "Gothic Revival architecture") style consecrated in 1912. After the diamond rush of 1908 and the completion of the railway line to [Keetmanshoop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keetmanshoop "Keetmanshoop"), Lüderitz became permanently home to a significant white population. As a result, a number of churches were built. Felsenkirche, one of the oldest [Lutheran churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheran_church "Lutheran church") in Namibia, has been a national monument since 1978.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-31)
*   **Glück Auf** building, built 1907/08 for a lawyer of the diamond companies, declared a national monument in 2014[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-new-30)
*   **Goerkehaus**, the residence of Hans Goerke, manager and co-owner of the early diamond umbrella company, erected 1909–1911,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-L%C3%BCderitzbucht-6) national monument[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-new-30)
*   **Kreplinhaus**, the residence of the first mayor, Emil Kreplin, built in 1909,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-L%C3%BCderitzbucht-6) national monument[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-new-30)
*   **Krabbenhöft & Lampe** building, after co-owners Friedrich Wilhelm Krabbenhöft and Oscar Lampe. The predecessor of this business, the _Handelsstation F.W. Krabbenhöft_ in Keetmanshoop, had existed since 1880 and was one of the first formally registered businesses in South West Africa. Erection of the building started in late 1909 and has been a national monument since 1979.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-32)
*   **[Lüderitz Railway Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%BCderitz_Railway_Station "Lüderitz Railway Station")**, erected in 1904,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-L%C3%BCderitzbucht-6) is also a national monument.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luderitz#cite_note-new-30)

# We contine the long drive to Luderitz

Posted on January 20, 2018 July 1, 2025Likes LikeCategories Africa Author by [Vicky Ireland](https://travellinlite.co.za/author/vicky/)Tags Deadvlei, Klein-Aus-Vista, Le Mirage, Luderitz, Oryx, Wild horses

* * *

As the crow flies, the distance between [Swakopmund](https://www.lonelyplanet.com/namibia/western-namibia/swakopmund)and [Luderitz](https://travellinlite.co.za/we-contine-the-long-drive-to-luderitz/namibian.org/travel/namibia/luderitz.htm) is about 450kms but one can only go this route along the coast if part of a safari tour. We had to travel the long way around which was 800kms. We decided to do this trip over 4 days stopping at both[Le Mirage Lodge](https://travellinlite.co.za/we-contine-the-long-drive-to-luderitz/namibian.org/travel/namibia/luderitz.htm)near [Sossuvlei](https://sossusvlei.com/en)/[Sesriem](https://www.sossusvlei.org/attractions/sesriem-canyon) and then at Klein-Aus-Vista.

![Image 4: Entrance to Le Mirage](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Entrance_to_Le_Mirage.jpg)

**Le Mirage Lodge**

On the way to Le Mirage, we again stopped at [Solitaire](https://www.solitairenamibia.com/), the little town with the restaurant which makes divine apple crumble. On the way there we crossed over the Tropic of Capricorn, another milestone of our visits to Namibia. For some reason I do not recall seeing the sign when we travelled from [Fish River Canyon](https://www.info-namibia.com/.../fish-river/fish-river-canyon)to [Gobabis](https://www.info-namibia.com/.../omaheke/gobabis) a few years earlier.![Image 5: V T having apple crumble](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/V__T_having_apple_crumble.jpg)

**Eating Apple Crumble at Solitaire**

![Image 6: Vicky Trevor at sign for Solitaire](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Vicky__Trevor_at_sign_for_Solitaire.jpg)

**Entrance to Solitaire which records the growing population on the little board below**

On the way to Le Mirage, we stopped at Sossuvlei/Sesriem once again. This time we first stopped at Dune 9 and another smaller dune, both of which Lyn and Trevor climbed, while I explored the surrounding area. From there we went to an area known as Dead Vlei, a dry section which is covered with dead trees. In a way I was reminded of Lake Kariba where the dead trunks of trees stand out of the water but here it was bone dry. There was an eerie feel to the place, but it was beautiful to see the different colours of the dunes and the vlei.![Image 7: T almost at the top](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/T_almost_at_the_top.jpg)

**Trevor approaches the top of a dune**

![Image 8: V T at ent to Sossusvlei](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/V__T_at_ent_to_Sossusvlei.jpg)

**Trevor & Vicky at entrance to Deadvlei**

![Image 9: Lyn Vicky at Deadvlei](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Lyn__Vicky_at_Deadvlei.jpg)

**Vicky & Lyn on a dead tree trunk in Deadvlei**

We continued on to the Lodge which was quite beautiful. This is a Resort and Spa which looks like a castle architecturally and stands proud, alone in the desert. It is about 20kms from the Sesriem Gate to Sossusvlei and is the only lodge accommodation in such proximity to the Vlei. The layout is quite unusual in that the rooms are in separate but connected ‘towers’ set around the swimming pool. On returning to Sossusvlei the next morning we found it flooded even more than when wee first visited 3 years earlier, from heavy rains in the North.

![Image 10: Le Mirage pool area](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Le_Mirage_pool_area.jpg)

**Pool area**

During our second visit it had been bone dry. so we had seen it in all possible conditions. This time we were unable to get to the far side dunes which we had climbed before. We sat under the trees for lunch and Lyn & Trevor once again enjoyed feeding the Cape Sparrows but this time they were not too keen to sit on their hands or arms.

![Image 11: Folding petrified dunes](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Folding_petrified_dunes.jpg)

**Range of petrified dunes on road to Klein-Aus-Vista**

The next morning saw us on the road to Klein-Aus-Vista, a truly beautiful drive and we were very relaxed, totally unaware of what we were to experience over the next few days. On arrival I agreed to walk to our chalets so as to be able to direct them when they brought the car around as the chalets were on a hill with winding roads. Accommodation located I waited at the corner. I waited and waited and waited!!! Finally, they came around the corner and up the hill having been delayed due to having to change a flat tyre.

![Image 12: Our chalet up on a hill at KAV](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Our_chalet_up_on_a_hill_at_KAV.jpg)

**Our chalets at Klein-Aus-Vista**

We unpacked and then went out on a sunset drive, not to see wildlife, but to appreciate the beauty of the landscape as the sun set. We stopped and drank our sundowners on the side of a dune – very sophisticated setup with a folding pine table, a beautiful platter of finger snacks and wine, juice or other soft drink. There were just the 3 of us but there was enough for at least 10! The sunset made up for the very bumpy drive.

![Image 13: Sunset while having sundowners](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Sunset_while_having_sundowners.jpg)

**Sunset over the dunes**

![Image 14: Moon above the golden dune](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Moon_above_the_golden_dune.jpg)**The moon hovers over petrified dunes**

Next morning we left, with no idea of what lay before us. It was going to be a long day! What should have been a 2-hour drive became 6 hours to travel 128kms! It was a very exhausting day in the hot and dry desert. Our first stop on this road was a scheduled one – to see the [wild desert horses,](https://www.wildhorsesandmustangs.com/the-wild...)something of which I had not heard before. Their actual origin has not been confirmed but there are 2 possible theories,

![Image 15: Wild horses having final drink](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Wild_horses_having_final_drink.jpg)

**Wild horses at the watering hole**

The first is that during WW1, the Germans made a surprise attack on the Union of South Africa troops who were stationed at Garub and the noise of the bombs frightened the horses, causing them to flee. The other, more likely, scenario is that they were bred as work horses for the Diamond Mines in the Luderitz area and when that came to an end they were released into the desert. Considering the harsh conditions, with negligible grazing and water they have adapted amazingly well. They discovered where to find grazing and the watering hole where we were able to see them.

![Image 16: Wild horse rolls in the sand](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Wild_horse_rolls_in_the_sand.jpg)

**The horses roll in the sand to dispose of the sand fleas and other insects**

Besides the horses there were a number of birds, Oryx and Zebra and it was fascinating to watch how each group would wait for the others to have a drink before moving in for themselves.

![Image 17: Oryx witing to drink](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Oryx_witing_to_drink.jpg)

**Oryx waiting to drink**

![Image 18: Oryx ostrich at watering hole](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Oryx__ostrich_at_watering_hole.jpg)**Oryx and Ostrich at the watering hole**

Approximately an hour later we continued on the long, straight road to Luderitz but, after travelling another 60kms, Lyn heard a click, click in the engine and then the car lost all power. Trevor noticed that the car had overheated and so we had to stop. It was hot, it was dry and there was not another vehicle nor any residence in sight. What happened next on this long and quiet road was close to unbelievable. The story continues in the next blog.

![Image 19: Road to Luderitz](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Road_to_Luderitz.jpg)**The road to Luderitz**

# We contine the long drive to Luderitz

Posted on January 20, 2018 July 1, 2025Likes LikeCategories Africa Author by [Vicky Ireland](https://travellinlite.co.za/author/vicky/)Tags Deadvlei, Klein-Aus-Vista, Le Mirage, Luderitz, Oryx, Wild horses

* * *

As the crow flies, the distance between [Swakopmund](https://www.lonelyplanet.com/namibia/western-namibia/swakopmund)and [Luderitz](https://travellinlite.co.za/we-contine-the-long-drive-to-luderitz/namibian.org/travel/namibia/luderitz.htm) is about 450kms but one can only go this route along the coast if part of a safari tour. We had to travel the long way around which was 800kms. We decided to do this trip over 4 days stopping at both[Le Mirage Lodge](https://travellinlite.co.za/we-contine-the-long-drive-to-luderitz/namibian.org/travel/namibia/luderitz.htm)near [Sossuvlei](https://sossusvlei.com/en)/[Sesriem](https://www.sossusvlei.org/attractions/sesriem-canyon) and then at Klein-Aus-Vista.

![Image 4: Entrance to Le Mirage](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Entrance_to_Le_Mirage.jpg)

**Le Mirage Lodge**

On the way to Le Mirage, we again stopped at [Solitaire](https://www.solitairenamibia.com/), the little town with the restaurant which makes divine apple crumble. On the way there we crossed over the Tropic of Capricorn, another milestone of our visits to Namibia. For some reason I do not recall seeing the sign when we travelled from [Fish River Canyon](https://www.info-namibia.com/.../fish-river/fish-river-canyon)to [Gobabis](https://www.info-namibia.com/.../omaheke/gobabis) a few years earlier.![Image 5: V T having apple crumble](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/V__T_having_apple_crumble.jpg)

**Eating Apple Crumble at Solitaire**

![Image 6: Vicky Trevor at sign for Solitaire](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Vicky__Trevor_at_sign_for_Solitaire.jpg)

**Entrance to Solitaire which records the growing population on the little board below**

On the way to Le Mirage, we stopped at Sossuvlei/Sesriem once again. This time we first stopped at Dune 9 and another smaller dune, both of which Lyn and Trevor climbed, while I explored the surrounding area. From there we went to an area known as Dead Vlei, a dry section which is covered with dead trees. In a way I was reminded of Lake Kariba where the dead trunks of trees stand out of the water but here it was bone dry. There was an eerie feel to the place, but it was beautiful to see the different colours of the dunes and the vlei.![Image 7: T almost at the top](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/T_almost_at_the_top.jpg)

**Trevor approaches the top of a dune**

![Image 8: V T at ent to Sossusvlei](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/V__T_at_ent_to_Sossusvlei.jpg)

**Trevor & Vicky at entrance to Deadvlei**

![Image 9: Lyn Vicky at Deadvlei](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Lyn__Vicky_at_Deadvlei.jpg)

**Vicky & Lyn on a dead tree trunk in Deadvlei**

We continued on to the Lodge which was quite beautiful. This is a Resort and Spa which looks like a castle architecturally and stands proud, alone in the desert. It is about 20kms from the Sesriem Gate to Sossusvlei and is the only lodge accommodation in such proximity to the Vlei. The layout is quite unusual in that the rooms are in separate but connected ‘towers’ set around the swimming pool. On returning to Sossusvlei the next morning we found it flooded even more than when wee first visited 3 years earlier, from heavy rains in the North.

![Image 10: Le Mirage pool area](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Le_Mirage_pool_area.jpg)

**Pool area**

During our second visit it had been bone dry. so we had seen it in all possible conditions. This time we were unable to get to the far side dunes which we had climbed before. We sat under the trees for lunch and Lyn & Trevor once again enjoyed feeding the Cape Sparrows but this time they were not too keen to sit on their hands or arms.

![Image 11: Folding petrified dunes](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Folding_petrified_dunes.jpg)

**Range of petrified dunes on road to Klein-Aus-Vista**

The next morning saw us on the road to Klein-Aus-Vista, a truly beautiful drive and we were very relaxed, totally unaware of what we were to experience over the next few days. On arrival I agreed to walk to our chalets so as to be able to direct them when they brought the car around as the chalets were on a hill with winding roads. Accommodation located I waited at the corner. I waited and waited and waited!!! Finally, they came around the corner and up the hill having been delayed due to having to change a flat tyre.

![Image 12: Our chalet up on a hill at KAV](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Our_chalet_up_on_a_hill_at_KAV.jpg)

**Our chalets at Klein-Aus-Vista**

We unpacked and then went out on a sunset drive, not to see wildlife, but to appreciate the beauty of the landscape as the sun set. We stopped and drank our sundowners on the side of a dune – very sophisticated setup with a folding pine table, a beautiful platter of finger snacks and wine, juice or other soft drink. There were just the 3 of us but there was enough for at least 10! The sunset made up for the very bumpy drive.

![Image 13: Sunset while having sundowners](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Sunset_while_having_sundowners.jpg)

**Sunset over the dunes**

![Image 14: Moon above the golden dune](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Moon_above_the_golden_dune.jpg)**The moon hovers over petrified dunes**

Next morning we left, with no idea of what lay before us. It was going to be a long day! What should have been a 2-hour drive became 6 hours to travel 128kms! It was a very exhausting day in the hot and dry desert. Our first stop on this road was a scheduled one – to see the [wild desert horses,](https://www.wildhorsesandmustangs.com/the-wild...)something of which I had not heard before. Their actual origin has not been confirmed but there are 2 possible theories,

![Image 15: Wild horses having final drink](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Wild_horses_having_final_drink.jpg)

**Wild horses at the watering hole**

The first is that during WW1, the Germans made a surprise attack on the Union of South Africa troops who were stationed at Garub and the noise of the bombs frightened the horses, causing them to flee. The other, more likely, scenario is that they were bred as work horses for the Diamond Mines in the Luderitz area and when that came to an end they were released into the desert. Considering the harsh conditions, with negligible grazing and water they have adapted amazingly well. They discovered where to find grazing and the watering hole where we were able to see them.

![Image 16: Wild horse rolls in the sand](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Wild_horse_rolls_in_the_sand.jpg)

**The horses roll in the sand to dispose of the sand fleas and other insects**

Besides the horses there were a number of birds, Oryx and Zebra and it was fascinating to watch how each group would wait for the others to have a drink before moving in for themselves.

![Image 17: Oryx witing to drink](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Oryx_witing_to_drink.jpg)

**Oryx waiting to drink**

![Image 18: Oryx ostrich at watering hole](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Oryx__ostrich_at_watering_hole.jpg)**Oryx and Ostrich at the watering hole**

Approximately an hour later we continued on the long, straight road to Luderitz but, after travelling another 60kms, Lyn heard a click, click in the engine and then the car lost all power. Trevor noticed that the car had overheated and so we had to stop. It was hot, it was dry and there was not another vehicle nor any residence in sight. What happened next on this long and quiet road was close to unbelievable. The story continues in the next blog.

![Image 19: Road to Luderitz](https://travellinlite.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/Road_to_Luderitz.jpg)**The road to Luderitz**

## Luderitz a coastal town with a past

The sheer isolation of Luderitz, the curious way in which its colonial style buildings cling to the rocks overlooking the bay, on some days a deep iridescent blue, on others grey and stormy, the crispy fresh climate, fishing boats bobbing up and down on the Atlantic Horizon, penguins and seals diving beneath the waves, give the town a curious other world allure.

## What to see and do in Luderitz

A town seemingly disconnected with the rest of the world at the end of the road Luderitz is an old fishing town around a rugged harbour, the coastline hides seals, penguins, sharks, shipwrecks and diamonds... visit deserted Kolmanskop - the old mining town that was mysteriously deserted and now is being retaken by the desert as the remains of the old bowling alley and decaying houses hint at life before the disappearance of the inhabitants.

![Image 4: Luderitz Town](https://www.nwrnamibia.com/luderitz/luderitz-town.jpg)

## Explore Luderitz

Lüderitz is located in a desert region, but has a relatively mild climate due to its coastal location. It is known for its charming, German-influenced architecture, with a number of historic buildings and landmarks, such as the Lüderitz Lighthouse and the Goerke Haus Museum.  
 The town is also home to a number of natural attractions, such as the Bogenfels rock arch and the Kolmanskop Ghost Town, which is a former diamond mining town that has been abandoned and is now a popular tourist attraction.  
 In addition to its cultural and natural attractions, Lüderitz is also a hub for outdoor activities.

![Image 5: Diaz Point Luderitz](https://www.nwrnamibia.com/luderitz/diaz-point-luderitz.jpg)

## Why visit Luderitz?

Luderitz located in the Karas Region of southern Namibia is a small coastal town. However, despite its small size, Luderitz has a large variety of things to do - from visiting a ghost town in the desert or exploring the Art Nouveau architecture to kite surfing and observing wildlife.

Luderitz is a quirky and quaint town with interesting architect.Luderitz was founded in 1883 after Franz Adolf Lüderitz bought the land from the local Nama chief Joseph Frederiks. In 1909 after the discovery of diamonds in the area, the town started growing and quickly.   
 By 1912 the population of the town expanded to 1100 inhabitants. This area became a prohibited zone for diamond mining and it is still prohibited. Today Luderitz is a quiet town located on the windy coast of the Namib Desert with most tourists coming here to visit Kolmanskop - the Ghost Town.

Luderitz’ economic activity is centered on the port. The port was the only suitable harbor on Namibia’s coast until Walvis Bay’s incorporation in 1994. When visiting Luderitz, one will notice is distinctive German atmosphere and the colonial style bulidngs which reflect Art Nouveau architecture. Luderitz is a great place for rock lobster fishing as well as processing. Penguin colonies are also found on the nearby Halifax Island and beautiful flamingos can be seen on beaches south of Luderitz.

In the past, Kolmanskop was a booming town built around diamond mines but it was completely abandoned for several decades until it was turned into an open-air museum.

The island is closed to the public but people are allowed to approach it on a catamaran to see the penguins. Besides penguins, visitors can see seagulls, cormorants and flamingos. Dolphins and seals are occasionally seen around the island.

 2. Discover Art Nouveau architecture - Goerke Haus is probably the most famous building in Luderitz. It’s a museum you can visit it and see its well-preserved interior. Luderitz is a small town with the historic buildings being situated close to each other so you can explore the town on foot.  
 3. Visit Shark Island - It offers beautiful views of Luderitz and the harbor. Around the island, you can see pelicans and seals.  
 4. Visit Diaz Point - Diaz Point named after Portuguese explorer Bartolomeu Dias whose expedition stopped in Luderitz on 25th July 1488 on his way back home. Dias Lighthouse, opened in 1915, is another attraction of Dias Point along with the cross.  
 5. Do a catamaran tour to Halifax Island - The Island is 100 m from the mainland. This small rocky island is known as home to one of the most important breeding colonies of the African penguin in Namibia. The island is closed to the public but people are allowed to approach it on a catamaran to see the penguins. Besides penguins, visitors can see seagulls, cormorants and flamingos. Dolphins and seals are occasionally seen around the island.  
 6. Observe wildlife at Grosse Bucht - A bay with a wild sandy beach about 20 km south of Luderitz. It’s a nice beach to go for a walk on but during summer it gets quite windy.   
 7. Go kite surfing  
 8. Visit Felsenkirche “rock church” - The prominent Felsen Kirche,an Evangelical Lutheran church dominates Lüderitz from high on Diamond Hill.  
 9. Visit the Luderitz Museum – The museum has information on the town’s history, displays on the natural history, local indigenous groups and the diamond-mining industry.

## Na ntína ya musé oyo

Musée Lüderitz oyo ezali na Namibia ezali eloko moko ya motuya mingi na makambo ya kala oyo ezali kopesa bato oyo bakendaka kotala engumba yango libaku ya koyeba makambo mingi oyo eleká mpe oyo etali bonkɔkɔ ya mboka yango. Talá makambo oyo bapaya bakoki kozela:  
  
Masano ya kala: Musée yango ezali kolakisa masano ndenge na ndenge oyo elobeli lisolo ya Lüderitz. Masano yango elobeli makambo ndenge na ndenge, na ndakisa ndenge engumba yango esalemaki, makambo oyo elekaki na eleko ya boyangeli, ntango bazalaki kobunda na diama, makambo oyo elekaki na mbu, mpe ndenge bato ya bamboka yango bazalaki ndenge na ndenge.  
  
Ndako ya bonkɔkɔ: Ndako yango ezali na ndako moko kitoko ya bonkɔkɔ ya bonkɔkɔ. Bato oyo bakendaka kotala ndako yango bakoki kosepela na ndenge oyo etongami mpe kotala biloko ndenge na ndenge oyo ezali na kati.  
  
Makambo ya bonkɔkɔ: Musée yango ezali na biloko ya bonkɔkɔ, bitika, bafɔtɔ, mikanda, mpe biloko oyo emonisi makambo oyo eleká na engumba yango, bomoi ya bato oyo bafandi kuna, mpe misala oyo esali ete engumba yango ezala malamu.  
  
Maritime Libula: Lokola Lüderitz ezali na libongo, mbala mingi na kati ya musée ezali na biloko ya kala Maritime, oyo ezali kolobela na mozindo makambo ya kala oyo elekaki na engumba yango, na ndakisa biloko oyo emonisi bato ya liboso oyo bazalaki kosala mibembo, masuwa oyo ebebaki mpe mombongo ya Maritime.  
  
Mayele ya koyeba makambo ya mboka: Ba-guide oyo bayebi makambo mingi mpe ba-displays oyo ezali kolakisa makambo mingi ezali kopesa ndimbola ya bomoi, mimeseno mpe mimeseno ya bato ya bikólo ndenge na ndenge oyo bafandi na etúká yango na boumeli ya bambula.  
  
Koyekola: Musée yango ezali kopesa bapaya libaku ya koyekola makambo ya ntina mingi ya istware ya engumba yango mpe koyeba makambo ya kala ya Namibia, yango wana ezali esika ya malamu mpo na bato oyo balingaka istware mpe bapaya.  
  
Na mokili mobimba, musée ya Lüderitz ezali kolakisa bato nzela moko na ntango, mpe ezali kosalisa bango báyeba makambo mingi oyo elekaki na engumba yango, bato na yango, mpe makambo oyo esalemaki na engumba yango. Ezali esika moko ya malamu mpo na bakɛngɛli ya zongazonga mpo na komitalela kati na kala mpe bokeseni ya mimeseno ya mboka Namibia.

## Na ntína ya musé oyo

Musée Lüderitz oyo ezali na Namibia ezali eloko moko ya motuya mingi na makambo ya kala oyo ezali kopesa bato oyo bakendaka kotala engumba yango libaku ya koyeba makambo mingi oyo eleká mpe oyo etali bonkɔkɔ ya mboka yango. Talá makambo oyo bapaya bakoki kozela:  
  
Masano ya kala: Musée yango ezali kolakisa masano ndenge na ndenge oyo elobeli lisolo ya Lüderitz. Masano yango elobeli makambo ndenge na ndenge, na ndakisa ndenge engumba yango esalemaki, makambo oyo elekaki na eleko ya boyangeli, ntango bazalaki kobunda na diama, makambo oyo elekaki na mbu, mpe ndenge bato ya bamboka yango bazalaki ndenge na ndenge.  
  
Ndako ya bonkɔkɔ: Ndako yango ezali na ndako moko kitoko ya bonkɔkɔ ya bonkɔkɔ. Bato oyo bakendaka kotala ndako yango bakoki kosepela na ndenge oyo etongami mpe kotala biloko ndenge na ndenge oyo ezali na kati.  
  
Makambo ya bonkɔkɔ: Musée yango ezali na biloko ya bonkɔkɔ, bitika, bafɔtɔ, mikanda, mpe biloko oyo emonisi makambo oyo eleká na engumba yango, bomoi ya bato oyo bafandi kuna, mpe misala oyo esali ete engumba yango ezala malamu.  
  
Maritime Libula: Lokola Lüderitz ezali na libongo, mbala mingi na kati ya musée ezali na biloko ya kala Maritime, oyo ezali kolobela na mozindo makambo ya kala oyo elekaki na engumba yango, na ndakisa biloko oyo emonisi bato ya liboso oyo bazalaki kosala mibembo, masuwa oyo ebebaki mpe mombongo ya Maritime.  
  
Mayele ya koyeba makambo ya mboka: Ba-guide oyo bayebi makambo mingi mpe ba-displays oyo ezali kolakisa makambo mingi ezali kopesa ndimbola ya bomoi, mimeseno mpe mimeseno ya bato ya bikólo ndenge na ndenge oyo bafandi na etúká yango na boumeli ya bambula.  
  
Koyekola: Musée yango ezali kopesa bapaya libaku ya koyekola makambo ya ntina mingi ya istware ya engumba yango mpe koyeba makambo ya kala ya Namibia, yango wana ezali esika ya malamu mpo na bato oyo balingaka istware mpe bapaya.  
  
Na mokili mobimba, musée ya Lüderitz ezali kolakisa bato nzela moko na ntango, mpe ezali kosalisa bango báyeba makambo mingi oyo elekaki na engumba yango, bato na yango, mpe makambo oyo esalemaki na engumba yango. Ezali esika moko ya malamu mpo na bakɛngɛli ya zongazonga mpo na komitalela kati na kala mpe bokeseni ya mimeseno ya mboka Namibia.

## Abstract

Portuguese voyages of discovery in search of a route to India led further and further south along the coastline of Africa. The discovery of a sea route to the countries of South Asia, then generally referred to as the 'Indies', was a chief priority of the Kingdom of Portugal at the end of the Middle Ages. By the time of Henry the Navigator's death in 1460, the Portuguese had reached the Senegal River, and during the reign of King Afonso V the African, they travelled another 2000 miles, reaching the Gulf of Guinea and entering the southern hemisphere for the first time. Portuguese sailors initially marked the places discovered during pioneer expeditions with wooden crosses or inscriptions carved on trees. King João II decreed that these marks should be permanent and last for centuries. Diogo Cão was the first to carry these marker stones, called padrões. The three most successful Portuguese explorers set up a total of 11 padrões on the shores of Africa: Diogo Cão set up four, Bartolomeu Dias left three, and Vasco da Gama erected six padrões, but only four of them in Africa. In today's Namibia, near Lüderitz, Bartolomeu Dias erected a stone padrão on St James Day in 1488. The padrão stood in place for 300 years before it fell over, probably at the turn of the 18th and 19th centuries. Fragments of the broken stone marker were taken as curios in the following decades and ended up in private and public collections. Systematic excavations were carried out in 1953, resulting in the discovery of 12 large and 180 tiny fragments of padrão. These padrão fragments are currently in the National Museum of Namibia in Windhoek. Previously taken pieces of padrão are in museums in Cape Town, Lisbon and Greenwich. A replica now stands in the place of the original padrão. This article traces the history of this padrão, the archaeological research conducted in 1953 and 1982, and considers its significance in its original sociopolitical context.

However, the current distribution of archaeological sites is limited to the southern margin of the Kalahari sediments in South Africa and to the northern part of Botswana. Surface scatters of archaeological artefacts in other parts of the Kalahari have not been studied systematically despite their potential to test human adaptation to marginal environments in the past. We developed a mobile Geographical Information System (GIS) setup that allows us to record the archaeological potential of Botswana's southwestern Kgalagadi district in a rapid and standardised manner. This paper describes five archaeological sites identified through our survey in the wider area around the town of Tsabong. Four of these sites, as well as the majority of identified surface archaeology, belong to the Middle Stone Age based on a first assessment of their lithic typology. A pattern is emerging of particular concentration of these sites on or near quartzite outcrops that are located next to pans. Additionally, six test pits confirmed the high potential for further archaeological investigations in this area using a landscape approach. This version of a paper published in a very truncated form in 2007 deals with the history of southern Mozambique in the second millennium AD and the problem of visibility of political and social processes in the archaeological record. An outline of the political history of Mozambique South of the Sabi /Save river between ca. 1100 AD and 1850 and a number of concepts are presented. The two main concepts are predatory expansion and the lineage state which dominated in the area and includes a kind of class formation. A better understanding of institutions and dynamics of the lineage state and the processes of predatory expansion will help archaeologists or even modern historians not familiar with these institutions to understand certain mechanisms and process sequences. Among the causes of internal dynamics are differences between richer and poorer in a political community as well as pressures to exploit all local resources which led to specializations and regional trade. The history presented here has in part been reconstructed on the basis of information mainly based on observations given by travelers and colonial officials between ca. 1500 and 1910 and oral evidence collected from about 1505 and 1730 onwards and registered in written documents. Oral History and written records permit us to reconstruct the existence of states like that of the Bashika and/ or Sono-Hlungwana, Cawuke, Gwambe, Tembe, and Gaza. We can also trace movements of groups identified as having originated in "Baatwa" or Nguni and Sotho, "Kalanga," or Venda areas. Lineage and conquest states are often not archaeologically visible. Visible may be the capital as structure if stone was used for building and possibly a central society supporting and organizing the state. What is traceable in geographical space and time horizons between the 18 th and the early 20 th century through pottery seem to be moment of predatory expansion of relatively egalitarian societies, that is, certain types of migration and conquest of groups who may even have occupied some of the pottery production centres near good clay deposits. In parts of Southern Mozambique there were documented massive population movements in the 18 th (and possibly also 17 th ) century, 50 to 150 years before the better known mfecane of the 19 th century. There are also traces of pre-17 th century processes in the evidence, possibly in the 11 th , 12 th and 15 th centuries. One or two of these older migration processes which were different in scale from the Gaza state formation seem to become visible partly if we map the distribution of decoration motives and other traits like elements of the profile and pot types. This paper will try to help to bridge what is still a gap in knowledge about the past known to a few specialists and popular ideas about the visibility of past empires or ethnic groups and encourage archaeologists to take a closer and more confident and informed look at history and past political structures. Abstract/Resumo Esta é versão mais completa de um artigo publicada em forma truncada em 2007. Trata da história de sul de Moçambique no segundo milénio da nossa e o problema de visibilidade de processos políticos e sociais nos dados arqueológicos, especialmente olaria. Apresentamos um esboço da história política de Moçambique ao sul do Save entre ca. 1100 e 1850 e um certo número de conceitos. Os principais conceitos são expansão predatória e o Estado Linhageiro que dominava nesta área e inclui uma variante de formação de classes. Um conhecimento melhor das instituições e dinámicas do Estado Linhageiro e dos processos de expansão predatória vai ajudar arqueólogos e até historiadores modernos que não estão familiarizados com estas instituicões de compreender mecanismos e sequências de processos. Entre as causas das dinámicas internas são as diferenças entre os mais ricos e pobres numa comunidade política bem como as pressões de explorar todos os recursos locais que levou a especializações e comércio regional. A história apresentada aqui foi em parte reconstruída na base de informações fornecidas por observações dadas por viajantes e oficiais coloniais entre cerca de 1500 e 1910 bem como fontes orais recolhidas a partir de 1505 e 1730 e registadas em fontes escritas. História oral e fontes escritas permitem reconstituir a existência de estados como os dos Bashika e/ou Sono-Hlungwana, Cawuke, Gwambe, Tembe, e de Gaza. Podemos traçar também movimentos de grupos que foram identificados como tendo originado em "Baatwa" (que se pode ter referido a área Nguni e Sotho), "Kalanga," ou na zona dos Venda. Em muitos casos os estados linhageiros não são visíveis no registo arqueológico. Visíveis podem estar a capital como estrutura, quando foi utilizado pedra para a construção e possivelmente uma sociedade central, que apoia e organiza o estado. Nos levantamentos feitos até agora sobressai no espaço geográfico estudado nos séculos XVIII a XX uma olaria que parece ter sido o produto de uma expansão predatória de sociedades relativamente igualitárias. Estas migrações e conquistas podem até ter ocupado alguns dos centros de produção de olaria. Em partes do Sul de Moçambique existiram movimentos maciços de populações no séc. XVIII, talvez já no séc. XVII, 50 a 150 anos antes dos mfecane do séc. XIX que são melhor conhecidos. Existem ainda traços de processos antes do séc. XVII, talvez no séc. XI, XII e XV. Um ou dois dos antigos processos de migração, que parecem ser diferentes em escala da formação do estado de Gaza parecem tornar-se visíveis se cartografamos a distribuição de motivos de decoração e outros traços como elementos do perfil e de tipos de vasos. Este artigo quer ajudar a fazer uma ponte sobre o espaço vazio que existe entre o conhecimento do passado por alguns especialistas e ideias populares sobre a visibilidade de estados e impérios antigos ou grupos étnicos e encoraja arqueólogos de estudar história e estruturas políticas do passado com mais atenção e confiança.

## Abstract

Portuguese voyages of discovery in search of a route to India led further and further south along the coastline of Africa. The discovery of a sea route to the countries of South Asia, then generally referred to as the 'Indies', was a chief priority of the Kingdom of Portugal at the end of the Middle Ages. By the time of Henry the Navigator's death in 1460, the Portuguese had reached the Senegal River, and during the reign of King Afonso V the African, they travelled another 2000 miles, reaching the Gulf of Guinea and entering the southern hemisphere for the first time. Portuguese sailors initially marked the places discovered during pioneer expeditions with wooden crosses or inscriptions carved on trees. King João II decreed that these marks should be permanent and last for centuries. Diogo Cão was the first to carry these marker stones, called padrões. The three most successful Portuguese explorers set up a total of 11 padrões on the shores of Africa: Diogo Cão set up four, Bartolomeu Dias left three, and Vasco da Gama erected six padrões, but only four of them in Africa. In today's Namibia, near Lüderitz, Bartolomeu Dias erected a stone padrão on St James Day in 1488. The padrão stood in place for 300 years before it fell over, probably at the turn of the 18th and 19th centuries. Fragments of the broken stone marker were taken as curios in the following decades and ended up in private and public collections. Systematic excavations were carried out in 1953, resulting in the discovery of 12 large and 180 tiny fragments of padrão. These padrão fragments are currently in the National Museum of Namibia in Windhoek. Previously taken pieces of padrão are in museums in Cape Town, Lisbon and Greenwich. A replica now stands in the place of the original padrão. This article traces the history of this padrão, the archaeological research conducted in 1953 and 1982, and considers its significance in its original sociopolitical context.

[Gerhard Liesegang](https://eduardo-mondlane.academia.edu/GerhardLiesegang)

This version of a paper published in a very truncated form in 2007 deals with the history of southern Mozambique in the second millennium AD and the problem of visibility of political and social processes in the archaeological record. An outline of the political history of Mozambique South of the Sabi /Save river between ca. 1100 AD and 1850 and a number of concepts are presented. The two main concepts are predatory expansion and the lineage state which dominated in the area and includes a kind of class formation. A better understanding of institutions and dynamics of the lineage state and the processes of predatory expansion will help archaeologists or even modern historians not familiar with these institutions to understand certain mechanisms and process sequences. Among the causes of internal dynamics are differences between richer and poorer in a political community as well as pressures to exploit all local resources which led to specializations and regional trade. The history presented here has in part been reconstructed on the basis of information mainly based on observations given by travelers and colonial officials between ca. 1500 and 1910 and oral evidence collected from about 1505 and 1730 onwards and registered in written documents. Oral History and written records permit us to reconstruct the existence of states like that of the Bashika and/ or Sono-Hlungwana, Cawuke, Gwambe, Tembe, and Gaza. We can also trace movements of groups identified as having originated in "Baatwa" or Nguni and Sotho, "Kalanga," or Venda areas. Lineage and conquest states are often not archaeologically visible. Visible may be the capital as structure if stone was used for building and possibly a central society supporting and organizing the state. What is traceable in geographical space and time horizons between the 18 th and the early 20 th century through pottery seem to be moment of predatory expansion of relatively egalitarian societies, that is, certain types of migration and conquest of groups who may even have occupied some of the pottery production centres near good clay deposits. In parts of Southern Mozambique there were documented massive population movements in the 18 th (and possibly also 17 th ) century, 50 to 150 years before the better known mfecane of the 19 th century. There are also traces of pre-17 th century processes in the evidence, possibly in the 11 th , 12 th and 15 th centuries. One or two of these older migration processes which were different in scale from the Gaza state formation seem to become visible partly if we map the distribution of decoration motives and other traits like elements of the profile and pot types. This paper will try to help to bridge what is still a gap in knowledge about the past known to a few specialists and popular ideas about the visibility of past empires or ethnic groups and encourage archaeologists to take a closer and more confident and informed look at history and past political structures. Abstract/Resumo Esta é versão mais completa de um artigo publicada em forma truncada em 2007. Trata da história de sul de Moçambique no segundo milénio da nossa e o problema de visibilidade de processos políticos e sociais nos dados arqueológicos, especialmente olaria. Apresentamos um esboço da história política de Moçambique ao sul do Save entre ca. 1100 e 1850 e um certo número de conceitos. Os principais conceitos são expansão predatória e o Estado Linhageiro que dominava nesta área e inclui uma variante de formação de classes. Um conhecimento melhor das instituições e dinámicas do Estado Linhageiro e dos processos de expansão predatória vai ajudar arqueólogos e até historiadores modernos que não estão familiarizados com estas instituicões de compreender mecanismos e sequências de processos. Entre as causas das dinámicas internas são as diferenças entre os mais ricos e pobres numa comunidade política bem como as pressões de explorar todos os recursos locais que levou a especializações e comércio regional. A história apresentada aqui foi em parte reconstruída na base de informações fornecidas por observações dadas por viajantes e oficiais coloniais entre cerca de 1500 e 1910 bem como fontes orais recolhidas a partir de 1505 e 1730 e registadas em fontes escritas. História oral e fontes escritas permitem reconstituir a existência de estados como os dos Bashika e/ou Sono-Hlungwana, Cawuke, Gwambe, Tembe, e de Gaza. Podemos traçar também movimentos de grupos que foram identificados como tendo originado em "Baatwa" (que se pode ter referido a área Nguni e Sotho), "Kalanga," ou na zona dos Venda. Em muitos casos os estados linhageiros não são visíveis no registo arqueológico. Visíveis podem estar a capital como estrutura, quando foi utilizado pedra para a construção e possivelmente uma sociedade central, que apoia e organiza o estado. Nos levantamentos feitos até agora sobressai no espaço geográfico estudado nos séculos XVIII a XX uma olaria que parece ter sido o produto de uma expansão predatória de sociedades relativamente igualitárias. Estas migrações e conquistas podem até ter ocupado alguns dos centros de produção de olaria. Em partes do Sul de Moçambique existiram movimentos maciços de populações no séc. XVIII, talvez já no séc. XVII, 50 a 150 anos antes dos mfecane do séc. XIX que são melhor conhecidos. Existem ainda traços de processos antes do séc. XVII, talvez no séc. XI, XII e XV. Um ou dois dos antigos processos de migração, que parecem ser diferentes em escala da formação do estado de Gaza parecem tornar-se visíveis se cartografamos a distribuição de motivos de decoração e outros traços como elementos do perfil e de tipos de vasos. Este artigo quer ajudar a fazer uma ponte sobre o espaço vazio que existe entre o conhecimento do passado por alguns especialistas e ideias populares sobre a visibilidade de estados e impérios antigos ou grupos étnicos e encoraja arqueólogos de estudar história e estruturas políticas do passado com mais atenção e confiança.

During the last few decades, maritime archaeology has developed into an internationally accepted field of specialisation within the discipline of archaeology. It has, however, only gained academic recognition in Southern Africa since the late 1980s, when a lecturing post for maritime archaeology was established at the University of Cape Town. This resulted in initial efforts being focused on South Africa. Now, however, the time has come to expand the development of maritime archaeology to neighbouring countries. Due to various positive factors – including the presence of an important research potential as well as growing interest and positive contributions by some organisations and private individuals – Namibia provides a fertile ground to extend the field of operations. This article first summarises the objectives and methodology of maritime archaeological research in general; then it offers suggestions as to how to establish this research specialisation in Namibia, bearing in mind local circumstances.

Come explore Lüderitz’s deep connection to the sea like never before.

## Abstract

A black and white photograph shows four men standing around a column on a rocky outcrop, one in clerical dress, one in military uniform, and two more dressed in suits. The monument comprises a pitted stone column surmounted by a metal shield with the coat of arms of the king of Portugal and a metal cross inscribed with the name “Dom João” and the date “1485”. This column, known in Portuguese as a padrão, is a nineteenth-century replica of a fifteenth-century monument, shipped from the port of Belém in Lisbon in 1485 and erected on the Cabo Negro on the coast of modern-day Angola, only to be sent back from Angola to Lisbon in 1892. The original was (and still is) displayed in the ethnographic museum of the Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa alongside the remains or reconstructions of four other early padrões. The replica shown in this photograph was destroyed in 1975 by the independence movement in Angola, an episode of iconoclasm that is testament to the enduring association of this monument with colonial oppression. This article explores the afterlives of the padrões, with particular attention on the shifting significance of their inscriptions and heraldic insignia.

The purpose of this paper is to analyse a particularly influential case of memory continuity in Portugal, that of Padrão dos Descobrimentos. Spaces of collective memory (such as public monuments) raise questions about what we celebrate, remember or rescue from oblivion, providing an opportunity to rethink the trauma. As such, care for public spaces is associated with ethical and cultural values. One of the difficulties with certain monuments has to do with the fact that they recall actions that today we see as traumatic acts. Thus, it is important to reflect on a critical use of memory. On August 8, 2021, Padrão dos Descobrimentos was the subject of a graffiti. One of the sides of the monument could read: "Blindly sailing for money, humanity is drowning in a scarlet sea". A great controversy immediately arose around the meaning of this gesture, as well as the role played by a monument that, after being temporarily built in 1940 for the Portuguese World Exhibition, was, in its current version, inaugurated in 1960, on the occasion of the fifth centenary of the death of Infante D. Henrique. This episode reignited a deeper cleavage around the uses of history and memory, the Portuguese colonial past, and the role of the Padrão dos Descobrimentos as an instrument for the reproduction of nationalism. In this sense, and with the authors proposing a new theoretical frame of reference based on the thought of Arendt and Ricoeur, its critical reading becomes relevant.

Centring on a 2019 incident in which the statue was graffitied with the political statement 'Colonialismo é Fascismo', I arrive at this intervention first by framing graffiti deployed against commemorative sites tied to colonialism and slavery, then turning to Cabral's life, his Santarém statue, and its surrounding spatial elements-arguing how the commemoration can provoke critical responses, particularly in light of historical controversies I go on to unpack as attributable to the figure. In assessing the intervention, I argue that it establishes a countercelebratory narrative of Cabral and posit that the political text graffitied on the statue should not be dismissed as mere vandalism but rather understood as a reinscription and form of textual marginalia that is useful in exposing silences surrounding colonial and authoritarian legacies, thereby contributing to the decolonising of the statue.

[Paweł Kardasz](https://independent.academia.edu/Pawe%C5%82Kardasz)

The South African Archaeological Bulletin, 2023

Portuguese voyages of discovery in search of a route to India led further and further south along the coastline of Africa. The discovery of a sea route to the countries of South Asia, then generally referred to as the 'Indies', was a chief priority of the Kingdom of Portugal at the end of the Middle Ages. By the time of Henry the Navigator's death in 1460, the Portuguese had reached the Senegal River, and during the reign of King Afonso V the African, they travelled another 2000 miles, reaching the Gulf of Guinea and entering the southern hemisphere for the first time. Portuguese sailors initially marked the places discovered during pioneer expeditions with wooden crosses or inscriptions carved on trees. King João II decreed that these marks should be permanent and last for centuries. Diogo Cão was the first to carry these marker stones, called padrões. The three most successful Portuguese explorers set up a total of 11 padrões on the shores of Africa: Diogo Cão set up four, Bartolomeu Dias left three, and Vasco da Gama erected six padrões, but only four of them in Africa. In today's Namibia, near Lüderitz, Bartolomeu Dias erected a stone padrão on St James Day in 1488. The padrão stood in place for 300 years before it fell over, probably at the turn of the 18th and 19th centuries. Fragments of the broken stone marker were taken as curios in the following decades and ended up in private and public collections. Systematic excavations were carried out in 1953, resulting in the discovery of 12 large and 180 tiny fragments of padrão. These padrão fragments are currently in the National Museum of Namibia in Windhoek. Previously taken pieces of padrão are in museums in Cape Town, Lisbon and Greenwich. A replica now stands in the place of the original padrão. This article traces the history of this padrão, the archaeological research conducted in 1953 and 1982, and considers its significance in its original sociopolitical context.

The glorification of the historical monument -a European phenomenon that emerged during the first quarter of the 19th Century -occupied a place of great theoretical and iconographic importance in the Portuguese press. Through engravings, its image attained a power of synthesis, both in the creation of symbols and in the understanding of stylistic categories, becoming a major driving force behind the greater value that was given to the medieval architectural heritage and its consequent restoration. Despite being given a relatively ineffective and somewhat belated administrative and legal framework, the prestige and popularity of medieval monuments were sufficient to ensure a significant number of restoration works after 1840. ## Abstract

A black and white photograph shows four men standing around a column on a rocky outcrop, one in clerical dress, one in military uniform, and two more dressed in suits. The monument comprises a pitted stone column surmounted by a metal shield with the coat of arms of the king of Portugal and a metal cross inscribed with the name “Dom João” and the date “1485”. This column, known in Portuguese as a padrão, is a nineteenth-century replica of a fifteenth-century monument, shipped from the port of Belém in Lisbon in 1485 and erected on the Cabo Negro on the coast of modern-day Angola, only to be sent back from Angola to Lisbon in 1892. The original was (and still is) displayed in the ethnographic museum of the Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa alongside the remains or reconstructions of four other early padrões. The replica shown in this photograph was destroyed in 1975 by the independence movement in Angola, an episode of iconoclasm that is testament to the enduring association of this monument with colonial oppression. This article explores the afterlives of the padrões, with particular attention on the shifting significance of their inscriptions and heraldic insignia.

A HISTORY OF THE PADRÃO DE SÃO TIAGO AT LÜDERITZ

[Paweł Kardasz](https://independent.academia.edu/Pawe%C5%82Kardasz)

The South African Archaeological Bulletin, 2023

Portuguese voyages of discovery in search of a route to India led further and further south along the coastline of Africa. The discovery of a sea route to the countries of South Asia, then generally referred to as the 'Indies', was a chief priority of the Kingdom of Portugal at the end of the Middle Ages. By the time of Henry the Navigator's death in 1460, the Portuguese had reached the Senegal River, and during the reign of King Afonso V the African, they travelled another 2000 miles, reaching the Gulf of Guinea and entering the southern hemisphere for the first time. Portuguese sailors initially marked the places discovered during pioneer expeditions with wooden crosses or inscriptions carved on trees. King João II decreed that these marks should be permanent and last for centuries. Diogo Cão was the first to carry these marker stones, called padrões. The three most successful Portuguese explorers set up a total of 11 padrões on the shores of Africa: Diogo Cão set up four, Bartolomeu Dias left three, and Vasco da Gama erected six padrões, but only four of them in Africa. In today's Namibia, near Lüderitz, Bartolomeu Dias erected a stone padrão on St James Day in 1488. The padrão stood in place for 300 years before it fell over, probably at the turn of the 18th and 19th centuries. Fragments of the broken stone marker were taken as curios in the following decades and ended up in private and public collections. Systematic excavations were carried out in 1953, resulting in the discovery of 12 large and 180 tiny fragments of padrão. These padrão fragments are currently in the National Museum of Namibia in Windhoek. Previously taken pieces of padrão are in museums in Cape Town, Lisbon and Greenwich. A replica now stands in the place of the original padrão. This article traces the history of this padrão, the archaeological research conducted in 1953 and 1982, and considers its significance in its original sociopolitical context.

The glorification of the historical monument -a European phenomenon that emerged during the first quarter of the 19th Century -occupied a place of great theoretical and iconographic importance in the Portuguese press. Through engravings, its image attained a power of synthesis, both in the creation of symbols and in the understanding of stylistic categories, becoming a major driving force behind the greater value that was given to the medieval architectural heritage and its consequent restoration. Despite being given a relatively ineffective and somewhat belated administrative and legal framework, the prestige and popularity of medieval monuments were sufficient to ensure a significant number of restoration works after 1840. Literature on art, the press and manuscript sources of the period, sought to identify the principles to underlie the idea of restoration in Portugal between 1839 and 1925, as compared to models adopted throughout Europe. Although Portuguese artistic culture lagged far behind other European nations, the restoration of medieval religious architecture was common practice in Portugal at that time, both due to the idea that unity had always been one of the fundamental principles of architecture and because the cult of monuments stemmed from a mythical and symbolic production of national identity.

lightbulb About this topic

Namibian history encompasses the chronological study of the events, cultures, and societies that have shaped Namibia from prehistoric times to the present. It includes the impact of indigenous peoples, colonialism, the struggle for independence, and the development of the nation-state in the context of regional and global influences.

## Key research themes

### 1. How did German colonialism and its legacy shape Namibia's historical memory and land ownership conflicts?

This research area investigates German colonial rule in Namibia, particularly focusing on the Ovaherero genocide and how colonial memories and land dispossession continue shaping Namibia's sociopolitical dynamics. The theme is important because it elucidates how historical colonial acts still influence land reform debates, memory politics, and international negotiations between Namibia and Germany.

### 2. What role did Finnish missionary activity play in shaping cultural and religious transformations among the Owambo people in Namibia?

This theme explores how Finnish missionaries in the late 19th and early 20th centuries influenced the cultural, religious, and sociopolitical landscape of the Owambo region in Namibia. It focuses on conversion processes, cultural identity transformations, and how missionary activities intersected with colonial governance and indigenous leadership, contributing to both cultural change and indigenous agency.

### 3. How do indigenous Namibian communities navigate cultural preservation and identity amid colonial legacies and contemporary socio-political challenges?

This research area focuses on indigenous cultural heritage in Namibia, examining how communities have preserved traditional practices, resisted cultural minoritization, and dealt with the impacts of colonialism, missionary activity, and modern state policies. The theme is pertinent for understanding indigenous identity resilience, cultural revitalization efforts, and contemporary challenges posed by ethnopolitical dynamics.
